81089.e: White blood cells are also made in the red bone marrow. They fight off bacteria and viruses.
81089.m: White blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

81090.q: What are bones called that are often put into soup because of their marrow?
81090.e: Marrow bones are beef bones with a lot of bone marrow. They give the soup flavour.

81091.q: What are the lowest ribs called, which are not attached to the breastbone at the front?
81091.e: The 11th and 12th ribs end freely at the front in the muscles of the belly wall. That is why they are called floating ribs.
81091.m: The lowest ribs are floating ribs.

81092.q: What do you often have to take off before an X-ray?
81092.e: Metal strongly blocks X-rays and shows up as a bright patch on the image. It could hide something important.
81092.m: Metal gets in the way on an X-ray image.

81093.q: Which cloth can you use in first aid to keep an injured arm still?
81093.e: A triangular bandage belongs in every first aid kit. You tie it into a sling in which the arm can rest still.
81093.m: A triangular bandage keeps an injured arm still.

81094.q: Why does a ball fall down when you let go of it?
81094.e: The Earth pulls all things towards itself. That is why a ball falls down when you let go of it.
81094.m: The Earth pulls everything towards itself.

81095.q: Why don't people in Australia fall off the Earth?
a: The Earth pulls everything towards itself everywhere
The wind always blows from above there
81095.e: The Earth is a ball and pulls everything towards its centre. So for everyone on Earth, down is where the ground is.
81095.m: Everywhere on Earth, gravity pulls towards the ground.

81096.q: What keeps the Earth in its orbit around the Sun?
a: A magnet in the Earth's core
81096.e: The Sun is huge and pulls on the Earth. That is why the Earth circles the Sun and does not fly away.
81096.m: The Sun's gravity keeps the Earth in its orbit.

81097.q: Why does the air stay around the Earth and not fly off into space?
81097.e: Air is also pulled by the Earth. So a layer of air stays around the Earth that we can breathe.
81097.m: Gravity holds the air around the Earth.

81098.q: Which body in our solar system has the strongest gravity?
81098.e: The more mass a body in space has, the more strongly it pulls. The Sun has by far the most mass in the solar system.
81098.m: The Sun has the strongest gravity in the solar system.

81099.q: What is another word for gravity?
81099.e: Scientists also call gravity gravitation. The word comes from the Latin word for heavy.

81100.q: On which planet would you be heavier than on Earth?
81100.e: Jupiter is the largest planet and pulls much more strongly than the Earth. There, gravity would pull you down more than twice as strongly.
81100.m: Gravity is stronger on Jupiter than on Earth.

81101.q: Why is it hard work to walk up a mountain?
81101.e: When walking uphill, you have to lift your body upwards against gravity. That takes a lot of strength.

81102.q: What happens to the speed of a stone that falls from a tower?
81102.e: Gravity pulls the stone down during the whole fall. That is why it gets faster and faster.
81102.m: A falling stone gets faster and faster.

81103.q: What is falling called when only gravity acts and there is no air slowing things down?
81103.e: In free fall, only gravity acts. Completely without air, it happens for example in space or in a tube with no air in it.
81103.m: In free fall, only gravity acts.

81104.q: According to legend, which scientist dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
81104.e: Galileo Galilei studied how things fall more than 400 years ago. Whether he really used the Tower of Pisa for this is not certain.
81104.m: Galileo Galilei studied how objects fall.

81105.q: What is the jump called in which you fall into the depths on a stretchy rope?
81105.e: In a bungee jump, you first fall freely, then the stretchy rope slows the fall. In Switzerland you can jump, for example, from the dam in the Verzasca Valley, which is about 220 m high.
81105.m: In a bungee jump, a stretchy rope slows the fall.

81106.q: Why is a fall from a great height more dangerous than from a small height?
a: You are going faster when you hit the ground
The air is colder higher up
The ground is harder further down
You get heavier as you fall
81106.e: From a great height, you have much more speed when you land. That is why the impact is much harder.
81106.m: The further you fall, the harder the impact.

81107.q: What do you often feel in your tummy when a drop tower at the funfair suddenly shoots downwards?
81107.e: When falling fast, your body suddenly feels very light. Many people feel a tingling in their tummy.
81107.m: When falling, you often feel a tingling in your tummy.

81108.q: Why does a ball roll down a hill by itself?
81108.e: On a slope, gravity pulls the ball diagonally downwards. That is why it starts rolling without anyone pushing it.

81109.q: Where does a ball land if you drop it in a train travelling smoothly and steadily?
81109.e: Before you let go, the ball is moving at the same speed as you and the train. That is why it falls straight down in front of your feet.
81109.m: In a train moving steadily, a ball falls just as in a train standing still.

81110.q: Roughly when did Isaac Newton live?
81110.e: Isaac Newton was born in 1643 and died in 1727. So that is more than 300 years ago.
81110.m: Isaac Newton lived more than 300 years ago.

81111.q: According to the story, what did Newton wonder when he saw an apple fall?
81111.e: Newton wondered why the apple always falls straight down and never sideways or upwards. This question got him thinking about gravity.
81111.m: A falling apple got Newton thinking.

81112.q: What did Newton realise about the apple and the Moon?
a: The same force acts on both
The Moon is a giant apple
Apples only fall at full moon
81112.e: Newton realised that the Earth's gravity pulls the apple down. The same force also keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth.
81112.m: Gravity pulls the apple and keeps the Moon in its orbit.

81113.e: Newton was a scientist. He worked mainly as a physicist and mathematician and was a professor at Cambridge.
81113.m: Isaac Newton was a physicist and mathematician.

81114.q: Does Newton's famous apple tree still exist today?
a: Yes, it still stands in England
No, it was only in a fairy tale
81114.e: An apple tree in the garden of the house in England where Newton was born is said to be this famous tree. It once fell over, but grew again from its roots.
81114.m: Newton's apple tree still stands in England today.

81115.q: Which instrument for observing the stars did Newton improve?
81115.e: Newton built a telescope with a mirror. Such reflecting telescopes are still built today.

81116.q: What did Newton show with a triangular piece of glass, a prism?
a: White light is made up of colours
81116.e: Newton sent sunlight through a prism. The light was split into the colours of the rainbow.
81116.m: White light is made up of many colours.

81117.q: What do you need a parachute for?
81117.e: Without a parachute, you would fall faster and faster. The parachute slows you down so much that you can land safely.
81117.m: A parachute makes a safe landing possible.

81118.q: What must a parachute have so that it slows you down well?
81118.e: A large surface has to push a lot of air out of the way as it falls. This slows the fall a lot.
81118.m: The larger the surface, the more the parachute slows you down.

81119.q: What are parachutes usually made of today?
81119.e: Parachutes are sewn from light, tear-proof synthetic fabric such as nylon. So they are light and still strong.
81119.m: Parachutes are made of light, strong fabric.

81120.q: Which famous artist drew a parachute more than 500 years ago?
81120.e: Leonardo da Vinci drew a pyramid-shaped parachute around the year 1485. Much later it was shown that it works.
81120.m: Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute very early on.

81121.q: Which plant sends its seeds through the air on little parachutes?
81121.e: Dandelion seeds hang from fine hairs like from a parachute. So they fly far away on the wind.
81121.m: Dandelion seeds fly on little parachutes.

81122.q: What is the wing called that lets you glide through the air down from mountains in Switzerland?
81122.e: With a paraglider, you take off from a slope and glide through the air for a long time. This is very popular in the Swiss mountains.
81122.m: With a paraglider you can glide through the air.

81123.q: How does a skydiver open their parachute?
a: They press a button on their helmet
They blow it up with their mouth
They open a zip on their tummy
81123.e: The parachute is folded up in a backpack. When the skydiver pulls a handle, the parachute comes out and opens.
81123.m: A handle on the backpack opens the parachute.

81124.q: What do some very fast racing cars use a parachute for?
81124.e: Very fast racing cars open a brake parachute after the finish. The air in the parachute slows the car down.
81124.m: A brake parachute can also slow down a car.

81125.q: What happens to a skydiver just after the parachute opens?
a: They spin round in a circle
81125.e: The open parachute fills with air and suddenly slows the fall a lot. Afterwards the skydiver sinks slowly to the ground.
81125.m: An open parachute slows the fall sharply.

81126.q: Which falls more slowly through the air: a feather or a stone?
81126.e: The feather is light and has a large surface for its weight. So the air slows it down much more than the stone.
81126.m: A feather falls more slowly through the air than a stone.

81127.q: What is the slowing effect of air on falling things called?
81127.e: A falling object has to push the air aside. This slows it down; it is called air resistance.
81127.m: Air resistance slows down falling things.

81128.q: What happened when an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time on the Moon in 1971?
a: Both landed at the same time
81128.e: There is no air on the Moon that could slow things down. That is why the hammer and the feather fell at exactly the same speed.
81128.m: Without air, a feather and a hammer fall at the same speed.

81129.q: What happens if you screw a sheet of paper up into a ball and drop it?
a: It falls faster than a flat sheet
It falls more slowly than a flat sheet
81129.e: The paper ball has a much smaller surface than the flat sheet. So the air slows it down less.
81129.m: A small surface is slowed down less by the air.

81130.q: What is a space with no air at all called?
81130.e: If you pump all the air out of a space, you get a vacuum. The word comes from the Latin word for empty.
81130.m: A space without air is called a vacuum.

81131.q: Why do downhill ski racers ski in a deep crouch?
a: So that the air slows them down less
So that they feel less cold
So that they can see better
81131.e: In a crouch, the skiers offer less surface to the air. So the air slows them down less and they go faster.
81131.m: In a crouch, the air slows you down less.

81132.q: Why is cycling hard work in a strong headwind?
a: The air slows you down more
81132.e: With a headwind, the air flows against you. You have to use more force to push against it.
81132.m: A headwind slows you down when cycling.

81133.q: Why does a leaf float slowly and swaying from the tree to the ground?
a: The air slows down the light leaf
The leaf is heavier than a stone
The tree holds on to it
The Earth does not pull leaves
81133.e: A leaf is very light and flat. The air slows it down a lot and makes it sway to and fro.
81133.m: Light, flat things are slowed down a lot by the air.

81134.q: What do you use to measure how heavy someone is?
81134.e: On scales, your body presses down. The scales show how heavy you are.
81134.m: You measure how heavy something is with scales.

81135.q: Why do you press down on the scales when you stand on them?
81135.e: Gravity pulls your body down. That is why you press on the scales, and they can show your weight.
81135.m: Gravity presses you onto the scales.

81136.q: Which is heavier: a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of stones?
81136.e: A kilogram is always a kilogram. The feathers just take up much more space than the stones.
81136.m: A kilogram of feathers is just as heavy as a kilogram of stones.

81137.q: In which unit is a person's weight usually given?
81137.e: Body weight is given in kilograms, kg for short. An 8-year-old child often weighs about 25 kg.
81137.m: Body weight is measured in kilograms.

81138.q: Why does a full school bag feel heavier than an empty one?
a: There is more in it, and the Earth pulls on it more strongly
The air presses harder on full bags
The straps get shorter as you fill it
81138.e: The more things there are in the bag, the more strongly the Earth pulls on it. That is why you have to hold a full school bag more firmly.
81138.m: The more there is in it, the heavier the bag.

81139.q: What happens to the spring of a spring balance when you hang something heavy from it?
81139.e: The heavy thing pulls the spring down. The heavier it is, the longer the spring gets.
81139.m: The heavier something is, the more it stretches the spring.

81140.q: What does a beam balance do when there is the same weight on both sides?
81140.e: On a beam balance, the heavier side goes down. If both sides are equally heavy, the beam stays level.
81140.m: With equal weight, a beam balance stays balanced.

81141.q: Which is heavier: a litre of water or a litre of air?
a: Air has no weight at all
81141.e: A litre of air weighs only about one gram. A litre of water weighs around a thousand times more.
81141.m: Water is much heavier than air.

81142.q: Is gravity on the Moon stronger or weaker than on Earth?
81142.e: The Moon pulls things much less strongly than the Earth. That is why everything on the Moon is much lighter.
81142.m: Gravity on the Moon is weaker than on Earth.

81143.q: How high can an astronaut jump on the Moon?
a: Just as high as on Earth
81143.e: The Moon pulls much more weakly than the Earth. That is why you can jump much higher there.
81143.m: On the Moon you jump much higher.

81144.q: How does a heavy rucksack feel on the Moon?
81144.e: The Moon pulls things much more weakly than the Earth. That is why a rucksack feels much lighter there.
81144.m: On the Moon everything feels much lighter.

81145.q: What do astronauts on the Moon need to breathe?
81145.e: There is almost no air on the Moon. That is why astronauts wear a spacesuit that gives them air to breathe.
81145.m: On the Moon you need a spacesuit to breathe.

81146.q: Why is gravity on the Moon weaker than on Earth?
a: The Moon is much smaller and lighter
The Moon is further from the Sun
It is dark on the Moon
81146.e: The more mass a body in space has, the more strongly it pulls. The Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth.
81146.m: The small Moon pulls more weakly than the big Earth.

81147.q: How does a stone fall on the Moon compared with on Earth?
81147.e: Because the Moon pulls more weakly, a falling stone speeds up more slowly there than on Earth. It takes longer to reach the ground.
81147.m: On the Moon things fall more slowly than on Earth.

81148.q: What does the Moon's pull do to the Earth's seas?
81148.e: The Moon pulls on the water of the seas. This makes the water level rise and fall regularly; these are the tides.

81149.q: What was the mission called that first landed people on the Moon in 1969?
81149.e: In July 1969, the Apollo 11 mission landed on the Moon. Two astronauts walked on the Moon's surface.
81149.m: With Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon in 1969.

81150.q: What do you call a person who flies into space?
81150.e: People who fly into space on a rocket are called astronauts.
81150.m: Someone who flies into space is an astronaut.

81151.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon, in 1969?
81151.e: Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon, in July 1969. He was an astronaut from the USA.
81151.m: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.

81152.q: Where do astronauts today often live in space for months at a time?
81152.e: The International Space Station, ISS for short, circles the Earth. People often live and do research there for half a year.
81152.m: People live in space on the ISS space station.

81153.q: Why do astronauts wear a spacesuit outside in space?
a: It gives them air and protects them
81153.e: In space there is no air to breathe, and it is very hot or very cold. The spacesuit supplies them with air and protects them.
81153.m: A spacesuit protects astronauts in space.

81154.q: Why do astronauts on the space station have to exercise every day?
a: Otherwise their muscles and bones get weak
So that they do not get bored
81154.e: Without gravity, muscles and bones hardly have to work and get weaker. With daily training, astronauts keep them strong.
81154.m: Astronauts train every day so that their muscles stay strong.

81155.q: Which sport did the astronaut Alan Shepard play on the Moon in 1971?
81155.e: Alan Shepard had taken a golf club and two golf balls to the Moon. In his stiff spacesuit he hit the balls with only one hand.
81155.m: Golf has been played on the Moon.

81156.q: What happens to astronauts' height in space?
81156.e: Without gravity, the spine is not squashed together and stretches a little. Back on Earth they get shorter again.
81156.m: In space, astronauts get a little taller.

81157.q: How long does the International Space Station take to go once around the Earth?
a: About an hour and a half
81157.e: The ISS flies very fast. It circles the Earth in around 90 minutes, so about 16 times a day.
81157.m: The ISS circles the Earth in about an hour and a half.

81158.q: What happens to a pencil that an astronaut lets go of on the space station?
a: It falls quickly to the floor
81158.e: On the space station, everything falls around the Earth together with the station. That is why things seem to float.
81158.m: On the space station things float.

81159.q: Why do astronauts sleep in a sleeping bag fixed to the wall?
a: So that they do not float around
So that they do not get cold
So that they do not snore
81159.e: Without the fixed sleeping bag, the astronauts would drift through the station in their sleep. This way they stay in their place.
81159.m: Astronauts sleep in fixed sleeping bags.

81160.q: What shape does a drop of water take in weightlessness?
81160.e: Without gravity, the water pulls itself together into a round ball. Such water balls float freely through the station.

81161.q: How does the toilet on the space station work?
a: It sucks things away with a stream of air
It flushes with lots of water
It works just like on Earth
There is no toilet at all
81161.e: In weightlessness, nothing falls down. That is why the toilet sucks everything away with a stream of air.
81161.m: The toilet in space works with a stream of air.

81162.q: Why do astronauts on the space station often eat tortillas instead of bread?
81162.e: Breadcrumbs would float around in weightlessness and could get into equipment or eyes. Tortillas hardly make crumbs.

81163.q: How can you experience weightlessness on Earth for a few seconds?
a: In an aeroplane flying an arc
In a lift that is standing still
81163.e: On a parabolic flight, an aeroplane flies a steep arc. For about 20 seconds the people inside float.
81163.m: On a parabolic flight you can float for a short time.

81164.q: What shape is a candle flame in weightlessness?
81164.e: On Earth, warm air rises and stretches the flame upwards. In weightlessness this does not happen, so the flame is round.
81164.m: In weightlessness a flame burns in a round ball.

81165.q: Why are tools on the space station often fixed with Velcro or cords?
a: So that they do not float away
So that they do not rust
81165.e: A tool that you let go of in weightlessness drifts away. With Velcro or cords it stays close by.
81165.m: On the space station, tools are fixed so that they do not drift away.

81166.q: What do you jump over in the high jump?
81166.e: In the high jump, a bar rests on two stands. You try to jump over it without knocking it off.
81166.m: In the high jump you jump over a bar.

81167.q: What is the well-known technique called in which you jump backwards over the bar?
81167.e: The American Dick Fosbury made this technique famous in 1968. Today almost all high jumpers jump like this.
81167.m: In the Fosbury flop you jump backwards over the bar.

81168.q: What do you land on in the high jump?
81168.e: Behind the bar there is a big, thick mat. It catches the jumpers softly.
81168.m: In the high jump you land on a thick mat.

81169.q: Why does every high jumper come back down after the jump?
81169.e: At take-off, you give yourself momentum upwards. Gravity slows this momentum and pulls the jumper back to the ground.
81169.m: Gravity brings every jumper back to the ground.

81170.q: Roughly how high is the men's high jump world record (as of 2025)?
81170.e: Javier Sotomayor from Cuba jumped 2.45 m in 1993. In 2025 this record had still not been broken.
81170.m: The men's high jump world record is about 2.45 m.

81171.q: Which sport does the high jump belong to?
81171.e: The high jump is an athletics event. Running, the long jump and the shot put also belong to it.
81171.m: The high jump belongs to athletics.

81172.q: In which kind of jump do athletes get much higher than in the high jump?
81172.e: In the pole vault, a bendy pole helps to fling the body high up. The best manage over 6 m.
81172.m: With a pole you jump much higher than without.

81173.q: What happens if the bar falls down in the high jump?
81173.e: The bar must stay in place after the jump. If it falls down, the attempt does not count.
81173.m: If the bar falls, the jump does not count.

81174.q: Why does the water in a waterfall plunge downwards?
81174.e: Gravity pulls the water down. Where there is a rock step, it plunges down.
81174.m: Gravity makes the water plunge down.

81175.q: What is the famous big waterfall near Schaffhausen called?
81175.e: At the Rhine Falls, the Rhine plunges over a wide rock step. It is one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.
81175.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

81176.q: Which valley in the Bernese Oberland has especially many waterfalls, for example the Staubbach Falls?
81176.e: In the Lauterbrunnen Valley, many streams plunge over the steep rock walls. The Staubbach Falls drop almost 300 m.
81176.m: The Lauterbrunnen Valley is famous for its waterfalls.

81177.q: Which waterfalls near Lauterbrunnen plunge down inside a mountain?
81177.e: The Trümmelbach Falls flow through gorges and caves inside the mountain. They carry meltwater from glaciers into the valley.
81177.m: The Trümmelbach Falls plunge down inside the mountain.

81178.q: In which country is the highest waterfall in the world, Angel Falls?
81178.e: Angel Falls is in Venezuela in South America. There the water falls almost 1000 m.
81178.m: The highest waterfall in the world is in Venezuela.

81179.q: On which lake in the Bernese Oberland do the Giessbach Falls plunge down in 14 steps?
81179.e: The Giessbach Falls flow down in 14 steps into Lake Brienz. There is also a well-known old hotel there.
81179.m: The Giessbach Falls plunge into Lake Brienz.

81180.e: A plumb bob is a heavy, pointed weight hanging from a string.
81180.m: A plumb bob is a weight on a string.

81181.q: What do bricklayers use a plumb bob for?
a: To check whether a wall is vertical
81181.e: The string of the plumb bob hangs exactly vertically. If you hold it next to a wall, you can see whether the wall is straight.
81181.m: With a plumb bob you check whether something is vertical.

81182.q: Which way does the string of a plumb bob point when it hangs still?
81182.e: When the plumb bob hangs still, the string points exactly straight down towards the Earth.
81182.m: The string of a plumb bob points straight down.

81183.q: Why does a plumb bob always hang straight down?
a: Gravity pulls the weight towards the Earth
81183.e: The Earth pulls the heavy weight towards itself. That is why the string points exactly towards the centre of the Earth.
81183.m: Gravity pulls the plumb bob down.

81185.q: What did sailors in the past use a lead weight on a long line for?
a: To measure the depth of the water
81185.e: The sailors lowered the heavy weight into the water until it touched the bottom. From the line they could see how deep the water was.
81185.m: With a weight on a line you measure the depth of the water.

81187.q: What do you call a line that points in exactly the same direction as the string of a plumb bob?
81187.e: The string of the plumb bob points straight down. Every line in this direction is a vertical.
81187.m: The string of a plumb bob forms a vertical line.

81188.q: Roughly how many Earths would fit inside Jupiter?
81188.e: Around 1300 Earths would fit inside Jupiter. That is how huge it is.
81188.m: Over a thousand Earths would fit inside Jupiter.

81189.q: Roughly how many times wider than the Earth is Jupiter?
81189.e: The Earth is just under 13,000 kilometres wide, and Jupiter around 143,000 kilometres. That is about eleven times as much.
81189.m: Jupiter is about eleven times as wide as the Earth.

81190.q: Who is the planet Jupiter named after?
a: The Roman god of the sea
81190.e: For the ancient Romans, Jupiter was the king of the gods. That is why the largest planet got his name.
81190.m: The largest planet has the name of the Roman king of the gods.

81191.q: Which planet is the second largest in our solar system?
81191.e: Only one planet is bigger than Saturn. Saturn is almost ten times as wide as the Earth.
81191.m: Saturn is the second largest planet.

81192.q: Who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610?
81192.e: In 1610 Galileo Galilei looked at Jupiter through a telescope. He saw four small points of light circling the planet.
81192.m: Galileo Galilei discovered the four large moons of Jupiter.

81193.q: On which moon of Jupiter are there especially many active volcanoes?
81193.e: Io has hundreds of volcanoes. No other place in the solar system has so many volcanic eruptions.
81193.m: Jupiter's moon Io is full of volcanoes.

81194.q: What is the name of the NASA space probe that arrived at Jupiter in 2016?
81194.e: The Juno space probe arrived at Jupiter in July 2016. Since then it has been exploring the giant planet up close.

81195.q: How heavy is Jupiter compared with all the other planets?
a: Heavier than all the others put together
81195.e: Jupiter has more than twice as much mass as all the other planets put together.
81195.m: Jupiter is heavier than all the other planets put together.

81196.q: Are Saturn's rings a solid disc?
a: No, just colourful rays of light
81196.e: The rings are made of countless separate chunks. Each chunk circles the planet on its own.
81196.m: Saturn's rings are made of many separate chunks.

81197.q: How thick are Saturn's rings compared with how wide they are?
a: Exactly as thick as they are wide
81197.e: The rings are hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide. But they are usually only about 10 metres to 1 kilometre thick.
81197.m: Saturn's rings are hugely wide but very thin.

81198.q: Why could Saturn's rings hardly be seen from Earth in March 2025?
a: We were looking exactly at their edge
81198.e: Every few years we look at the thin rings exactly from the side. Then they are almost invisible.
81198.m: From the side, Saturn's thin rings are almost invisible.

81199.q: Which other planet also has rings, but only very faint ones?
81199.e: Uranus has rings too. But they are dark and narrow and were only discovered in 1977.
81199.m: Saturn is not the only planet with rings.

81200.q: What was the name of the space probe that orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017?
81200.e: The Cassini space probe took pictures of Saturn, its rings and its moons for 13 years.
81200.m: The Cassini probe explored Saturn for many years.

81201.q: Can you see Saturn's rings with just a small telescope?
a: No, only with a space probe
81201.e: Even a small telescope shows the rings. You can often look at them yourself at an observatory.
81201.m: You can see Saturn's rings with a telescope.

81202.q: How many Earths side by side would fit across Saturn's bright rings?
81202.e: The bright rings are around 270,000 kilometres wide from edge to edge. That is about 20 Earths side by side.
81202.m: Saturn's rings are much wider than the Earth.

81203.q: Who was the first to realise in 1655 that Saturn has a ring?
81203.e: Christiaan Huygens was a scientist from the Netherlands. With his better telescope he recognised the ring around Saturn.

81204.q: Which god is Mars named after?
a: The Roman god of the sea
The Roman king of the gods
81204.e: The red colour reminded people of blood and war. That is why the planet was given the name of Mars, the god of war.
81204.m: Mars has the name of the Roman god of war.

81205.q: What are the two small moons of Mars called?
81205.e: Phobos and Deimos are small, lumpy moons. Their names mean “fear” and “terror”.
81205.m: The moons of Mars are called Phobos and Deimos.

81206.q: Roughly how long is a year on Mars?
81206.e: Mars takes 687 days to go once around the Sun. That is almost two Earth years.
81206.m: A Mars year is almost two Earth years long.

81207.q: How long is a day on Mars?
81207.e: Mars spins once around itself in 24 hours and 37 minutes. That is only a little longer than an Earth day.
81207.m: A day on Mars is almost as long as a day on Earth.

81208.q: What is there at the poles of Mars?
81208.e: At the north pole and the south pole of Mars there are caps of ice. You can see them as white patches.
81208.m: Mars has ice at its poles too.

81210.q: What colour is the sky at sunset on Mars?
81210.e: The fine dust on Mars makes blue light glow around the Sun. Photos from Mars rovers show this.
81210.m: On Mars the sunset glows bluish.

81211.q: How big is Mars compared with the Earth?
81211.e: Mars is around 6800 kilometres wide, and the Earth just under 13,000 kilometres.
81211.m: Mars is about half as wide as the Earth.

81212.q: What can sometimes cover the whole of Mars for weeks?
81212.e: On Mars there are dust storms that cover the whole planet. Then you can hardly see the surface any more.
81212.m: Huge dust storms sometimes rage on Mars.

81213.q: How big is the Great Red Spot compared with the Earth?
81213.e: The huge storm is wider than our whole Earth. In 2017 it was around 16,000 kilometres wide, while the Earth is just under 13,000 kilometres wide.
81213.m: The Great Red Spot is bigger than the Earth.

81214.q: Since when have people been watching the Great Red Spot on Jupiter without a break?
81214.e: The storm has been watched continuously since 1878. So it has been raging for over 140 years.
81214.m: The Great Red Spot is an ancient storm.

81215.q: How has the Great Red Spot been changing for many years?
81215.e: Around 1880 the spot was around 40,000 kilometres long. Today it is much smaller.
81215.m: The Great Red Spot is slowly shrinking.

81217.q: Roughly how long does the Great Red Spot take to turn once?
81217.e: The huge whirl takes a few Earth days to turn once. Depending on the year, about four to six days have been measured.
81217.m: The Great Red Spot turns once in a few days.

81218.q: How fast can the winds at the edge of the Great Red Spot be?
81218.e: Winds of over 400 kilometres per hour have been measured at the edge of the whirl. That is much stronger than any storm on Earth.
81218.m: Mighty winds rage in the Great Red Spot.

81219.q: Do scientists know exactly why the Great Red Spot is red?
a: No, it is not yet fully clear
Yes, it is made of rust
Yes, it is made of red soil
Yes, it is full of lava
81219.e: The cause of the colour is not yet known for certain. Probably substances high up in the clouds colour the storm red.
81219.m: The red colour of the spot is still a mystery.

81220.q: What is the highest volcano in the whole solar system called?
81220.e: Olympus Mons is a huge volcano on Mars. No other known volcano is higher.
81220.m: Olympus Mons is the highest volcano in the solar system.

81221.q: Roughly how high is Olympus Mons?
81221.e: Olympus Mons rises around 22 kilometres high. That is about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest.
81221.m: Olympus Mons is more than 20 kilometres high.

81222.q: How wide is the base of Olympus Mons compared with Switzerland?
a: Wider than the whole of Switzerland
As wide as a football pitch
81222.e: The base of the volcano is almost 600 kilometres wide. From west to east, Switzerland is only about 350 kilometres wide.
81222.m: Olympus Mons is wider than the whole of Switzerland.

81223.q: Which mountain on Earth is Olympus Mons named after?
81223.e: Mount Olympus is a mountain in Greece. According to the old legends, the Greek gods lived there.
81223.m: Olympus Mons is named after Olympus, the mountain of the gods.

81224.q: Why could Olympus Mons become so huge?
a: It rains a lot on Mars
Mars is bigger than the Earth
81224.e: On Mars, gravity does not pull as strongly. That is why so much lava could pile up there into a huge mountain.
81224.m: Because of the weak gravity, Olympus Mons grew so big.

81225.q: What is Olympus Mons on Mars?
a: The highest volcano in the solar system
81225.e: Olympus Mons is a huge shield volcano and over 20 km high. That is more than twice as high as Mount Everest.
81225.m: Olympus Mons is the highest volcano in the solar system.

81226.q: What is at the top of the summit of Olympus Mons?
81226.e: At the top of the volcano is a collapsed crater. It is up to 90 kilometres wide.
81226.m: There is a huge crater on the summit of Olympus Mons.

81227.q: How many dwarf planets are officially recognised (as of 2025)?
81227.e: The recognised ones are Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. But scientists think there are many more.
81227.m: There are five recognised dwarf planets.

81228.q: Which dwarf planet orbits between Mars and Jupiter?
81228.e: Ceres is the largest body between Mars and Jupiter. It is about 940 kilometres wide.
81228.m: Ceres orbits between Mars and Jupiter.

81229.q: In which year did astronomers decide what a dwarf planet is?
81229.e: In 2006 astronomers from all over the world met in Prague. There they decided what a planet is and what a dwarf planet is.
81229.m: The group of dwarf planets has existed since 2006.

81230.q: What makes a dwarf planet different from a real planet?
a: It has not cleared its orbit
81230.e: A planet is so big that it has cleared its orbit of other chunks. A dwarf planet cannot do that.
81230.m: A dwarf planet shares its orbit with many other chunks.

81231.q: Which dwarf planet was discovered in 2005 and is almost the same size as Pluto?
81231.e: Eris orbits far out beyond Neptune. Its discovery led to the question of what a planet actually is.
81231.m: Eris is a dwarf planet very far out.

81232.q: Which body in space has no longer counted as a planet since 2006, but as a dwarf planet?
81232.e: For a long time Pluto was the ninth planet. In 2006 scientists declared it a dwarf planet.
81232.m: Pluto has been a dwarf planet since 2006.

81233.q: Where does the dwarf planet Ceres orbit the Sun?
a: In the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
81233.e: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It is the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system.
81233.m: Ceres orbits in the asteroid belt.

81234.q: Which dwarf planet is the widest?
81234.e: Pluto is just under 2400 kilometres wide. No other known dwarf planet is wider.
81234.m: Pluto is the widest dwarf planet.

81235.q: In which year was Pluto discovered?
81235.e: Pluto was found in 1930 in the USA on photos of the night sky.

81236.e: Venetia Burney from England was eleven years old. She suggested the name of the Roman god, and it was chosen.
81236.m: A girl gave Pluto its name.

81237.q: What shape is the large bright area on Pluto?
81237.e: Photos from 2015 showed a bright area of ice on Pluto in the shape of a heart.
81237.m: There is a big heart of ice on Pluto.

81238.q: What was the name of the scientist who discovered Pluto?
81238.e: Clyde Tombaugh worked at an observatory in the USA. He compared many photos of the sky and found a moving point of light.

81239.q: Is Pluto bigger or smaller than our Moon?
81239.e: Pluto is just under 2400 kilometres wide. Our Moon is almost 3500 kilometres wide.
81239.m: Pluto is smaller than our Moon.

81240.q: What is the largest moon of Pluto called?
81240.e: Charon is about half as wide as Pluto. The two circle each other like a pair.
81240.m: Pluto's largest moon is called Charon.

81241.q: How long does Pluto take to go once around the Sun?
81241.e: Pluto is very far away and slow. Since it was discovered in 1930, it has not yet completed one whole orbit.
81241.m: A year on Pluto lasts almost 250 Earth years.

81242.q: Roughly how cold is it on Pluto?
81242.e: Pluto is so far from the Sun that hardly any warmth gets there. Its surface is about minus 230 degrees.
81242.m: It is icy cold on Pluto.

81243.q: Which god is Pluto named after?
81243.e: Pluto is the Roman god of the underworld. The name fits, because it is dark and cold out there.
81243.m: Pluto has the same name as the Roman god of the underworld.

81244.q: Between which two planets is the asteroid belt?
81244.e: The asteroid belt is a wide ring of chunks of rock. It lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
81244.m: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.

81245.e: Asteroids are chunks of rock and metal. Like planets they orbit the Sun, but they are much smaller.

81246.q: Roughly how many larger asteroids are there in the asteroid belt?
81246.e: Scientists estimate that about 0.7 to 1.7 million asteroids larger than one kilometre orbit there.
81246.m: A huge number of chunks orbit in the asteroid belt.

81247.q: How heavy are all the asteroids in the belt put together?
a: Twice as heavy as the Moon
81247.e: All the chunks together have only about three per cent of the mass of our Moon.
81247.m: All the asteroids together are lighter than the Moon.

81248.q: Is flying through the asteroid belt usually dangerous for a space probe?
a: No, the chunks are spread far apart
Yes, you can never get through
81248.e: There are usually huge distances between the asteroids. Many space probes have already flown through without an accident.
81248.m: The asteroid belt is much emptier than you might think.

81249.q: Which asteroid is the brightest and can sometimes even be seen without a telescope?
81249.e: Vesta has a bright surface. That is why on good nights you can see it with the naked eye as a faint dot.

81250.q: The Dawn space probe visited Vesta and Ceres. Where do these two bodies orbit?
a: In the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
81250.e: Vesta and Ceres are the largest bodies in the asteroid belt. The Dawn probe first orbited Vesta and then flew on to Ceres.
81250.m: The Dawn probe visited two large bodies in the asteroid belt.

81251.q: What shape are most small asteroids?
81251.e: Small asteroids are too light to pull themselves into a ball. That is why they often look like potatoes.

81252.q: How big is the Sun on the planet trail on the Uetliberg?
a: Just under one and a half metres
81252.e: There the Sun is a yellow ball 1.39 metres across. It is a billion times smaller than the real Sun.
81252.m: On the Uetliberg planet trail the Sun is a big yellow ball.

81253.q: What does one metre on the planet trail on the Uetliberg stand for in real space?
81253.e: The planet trail is scaled down a billion times. So one metre of trail stands for a million kilometres.
81253.m: On the planet trail everything is a billion times smaller.

81254.q: How big is the Earth on a planet trail that is scaled down a billion times?
81254.e: The Earth is just under 13,000 kilometres wide. A billion times smaller gives about 1.3 centimetres, the size of a marble.
81254.m: In the model the Earth is only as big as a marble.

81255.q: How far is the Earth from the Sun if everything is scaled down a billion times?
81255.e: The real distance is around 150 million kilometres. A billion times smaller, that is about 150 metres.
81255.m: In the model the Earth is about 150 metres from the Sun.

81256.q: Roughly how long does it take to walk the whole planet trail on the Uetliberg?
81256.e: The trail leads from the Uetliberg to the Felsenegg. It takes about two hours.
81256.m: The planet trail on the Uetliberg is a lovely walk.

81257.q: Why does a planet trail need so much space?
a: The distances in space are huge
81257.e: In the model the planets are small, but far apart. That way you can see how empty space is.
81257.m: A planet trail shows how far apart the planets are.

81258.q: What do the planets on a planet trail look like compared with the Sun?
81258.e: The Sun is much bigger than all the planets. That is why the planets in the model are only small balls.
81258.m: Next to the Sun, all the planets look tiny.

81259.q: How far is Neptune from the Sun if everything is scaled down a billion times?
81259.e: Neptune is around 4.5 billion kilometres from the Sun. A billion times smaller, that is about 4.5 kilometres.
81259.m: In the model Neptune is several kilometres from the Sun.

81260.q: Which planet comes directly after the Earth, counting from the Sun?
81260.e: After the Earth comes Mars as the fourth planet.

81261.q: Which two planets are the Earth's neighbours?
81261.e: Venus orbits on the inside and Mars on the outside. They are the closest to the Earth.
81261.m: Venus and Mars are the Earth's neighbours.

81262.q: Which planet orbits between Mars and Saturn?
81262.e: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
81262.m: Jupiter orbits between Mars and Saturn.

81263.q: Which planet comes directly after Saturn, counting from the Sun?
81263.e: After Saturn comes Uranus and then Neptune.

81264.q: How many planets orbit closer to the Sun than the Earth?
81264.e: Mercury and Venus orbit inside the Earth's orbit. The Earth is the third planet.
81264.m: Only two planets are closer to the Sun than the Earth.

81265.q: In the memory aid “My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming”, each word stands for a planet. Which one does “Just” stand for?
81265.e: The first letter of each word shows a planet in the right order. “Just” begins with J, as in Jupiter.
81265.m: A memory aid helps you learn the order of the planets.

81266.q: Which planet orbits between Mercury and the Earth?
81266.e: Mercury is the first planet and the Earth the third. Venus lies in between.
81266.m: Venus orbits between Mercury and the Earth.

81267.q: How many planets orbit further out than Mars?
81267.e: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune orbit outside the orbit of Mars.
81267.m: Four more planets come after Mars.

81268.q: How many gas planets are there in our solar system?
81268.e: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the gas planets. They are the four outer planets.
81268.m: Our solar system has four gas planets.

81269.q: Which of these planets is NOT a gas planet?
81269.e: Mars has solid ground made of rock. The other three are huge balls of gas.
81269.m: Mars is not a gas planet.

81270.q: Can a space probe land on a gas planet?
a: No, there is no solid ground
81270.e: Gas planets have no solid surface. A probe would keep sinking deeper into the gases.
81270.m: You cannot land on a gas planet.

81271.q: Which two gases are Jupiter and Saturn mainly made of?
81271.e: Jupiter and Saturn are made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. These are the lightest gases.
81271.m: Gas planets are mainly made of hydrogen and helium.

81272.q: Why do Uranus and Neptune look blue?
a: Because they are full of seas
Because they are made of blue rock
81272.e: Their outer layer contains the gas methane. It absorbs red light, so the planets look blue.
81272.m: The gas methane makes Uranus and Neptune blue.

81273.q: Which planet has the most known moons (as of 2025)?
81273.e: In March 2025 many new moons were confirmed. Saturn now has 274 known moons.

81274.q: Which planet takes the longest to go once around the Sun?
81274.e: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years for one orbit. No planet is slower.
81274.m: A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.

81275.q: What are Uranus and Neptune also called, because they contain a lot of frozen water?
81275.e: Uranus and Neptune contain a lot of water, ammonia and methane. That is why experts call them ice giants.
81275.m: Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants.

81276.q: Which planet has the coldest atmosphere in the solar system?
81276.e: About minus 224 degrees has been measured in the atmosphere of Uranus. That is the coldest value of all the planets.

81277.e: The four inner planets have solid ground made of rock and a core made of metal.
81277.m: The four inner planets are rocky planets.

81278.q: Which is the largest rocky planet?
81278.e: Of the four rocky planets, our Earth is the largest and the heaviest.
81278.m: The Earth is the largest rocky planet.

81279.q: Which planet is almost exactly the same size as the Earth?
81279.e: Venus is about 12,100 kilometres wide, and the Earth about 12,700 kilometres. That is why it is called the Earth's sister planet.
81279.m: Venus is almost the same size as the Earth.

81280.q: On which planet does the Sun rise in the west?
81280.e: Venus spins the other way round from most planets. That is why the Sun rises in the west there.
81280.m: On Venus the Sun rises in the west.

81281.q: What lasts longer on Venus: a day or a year?
81281.e: Venus spins very slowly around itself. It takes 243 Earth days for one turn, but only 225 for one orbit of the Sun.
81281.m: On Venus a day is longer than a year.

81282.q: On which planet are there seas of liquid water on the surface?
81282.e: Only the Earth has oceans of liquid water today. That is why life is possible here.
81282.m: Only the Earth has seas of liquid water.

81283.q: Which planet speeds around the Sun the fastest?
81283.e: Mercury is closest to the Sun and therefore moves fastest. It races along at almost 48 kilometres per second.

81284.q: How cold does it get on Mercury at night?
81284.e: Mercury has almost no atmosphere to hold in warmth. During the day it gets over 400 degrees hot, and at night it is icy cold.
81284.m: On Mercury it is icy cold at night.

81285.q: Where are the rocky planets in our solar system?
a: On the inside, close to the Sun
Right on the outside, beyond Neptune
Spread out between the gas planets
81285.e: The rocky planets are the four inner planets. The gas planets come further out.
81285.m: The rocky planets orbit close to the Sun.

a: Flashes from a thunderstorm far away
81286.e: With heat lightning, you see the light of flashes that are very far away. They are completely normal thunderstorm flashes.
81286.m: Heat lightning comes from a distant thunderstorm.

81287.q: Why do you hear no thunder with heat lightning?
a: The storm is too far away
The wind blows the thunder away
81287.e: The sound of thunder does not travel as far as the light of the lightning. That is why you only see the flashes.
81287.m: You see distant light, but you do not hear distant thunder.

81288.q: When do we often see heat lightning in Switzerland?
81288.e: In Switzerland, thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. In the evening you can see their distant flashes well in the dark sky.
81288.m: You often see heat lightning on summer evenings.

81289.q: From what distance can you usually no longer hear a storm's thunder?
81289.e: You can usually only hear thunder up to about 15 to 20 kilometres away. You can see the light of lightning much further.

81290.q: With heat lightning, what do you often see instead of the flash itself?
a: The glow reflected in the clouds
81290.e: The flash itself is often hidden behind clouds or the horizon. You then only see the clouds light up briefly.
81290.m: With heat lightning, often only the clouds light up.

81291.q: Why do you mainly see heat lightning at night?
a: The faint glow stands out in the dark
The moon makes the clouds glow
81291.e: The distant glow is faint. In bright daylight you hardly see it, but in the dark night sky you see it well.
81291.m: You see heat lightning best in the dark.

81292.q: Where in the sky do you usually see heat lightning?
81292.e: The thunderstorm is far away. That is why it lights up low on the horizon.
81292.m: Heat lightning usually flickers on the horizon.

81293.q: What should you do if you suddenly hear thunder after seeing heat lightning?
a: Find shelter in a house or car
81293.e: If you can hear thunder, the storm is already close enough for lightning to strike. Then you find shelter at once.
81293.m: If you hear thunder, find shelter.

a: Rain with small grains of ice
81294.e: In drizzle, lots of tiny droplets fall. You hardly feel them one by one.
81294.m: Drizzle is made of very fine drops.

81295.q: How big are the droplets in drizzle?
81295.e: Drizzle droplets are tiny. Normal raindrops are usually much bigger.

81296.q: What does the sky usually look like when it is drizzling?
81296.e: Drizzle usually falls from a flat, grey layer of cloud that hangs low over the land.
81296.m: When it drizzles, the sky is grey.

81297.q: How do drizzle droplets fall compared with big raindrops?
81297.e: Small droplets are light and are strongly slowed down by the air. They almost float down.
81297.m: The smaller a drop is, the more slowly it falls.

81298.q: How long can it drizzle in Switzerland?
a: Only during a flash of lightning
81298.e: It can drizzle for a long time from a thick, low layer of cloud. Sometimes it does not stop for hours.
81298.m: Drizzle can last a very long time.

81300.q: How much water does drizzle usually bring?
81300.e: Because the droplets are so small, drizzle usually only adds up to a little water.
81300.m: Drizzle usually brings only a little water.

81301.q: How does drizzle feel on your skin?
81301.e: The droplets are so fine that you can hardly feel more than a damp breath of air.

81302.q: How hot does a flash of lightning get?
81302.e: A flash of lightning heats the air to about 30,000 degrees. That is much hotter than the surface of the sun.
81302.m: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.

81303.q: How long does a flash of lightning last?
81303.e: A flash of lightning only lasts a fraction of a second. Sometimes it flickers several times in quick succession.
81303.m: Lightning is over in a flash.

81304.q: What should you do if a thunderstorm comes while you are swimming?
a: Get out of the water at once
81304.e: In the water you are the highest point, and water conducts electricity. That is why you must get out at once in a thunderstorm.
81304.m: In a thunderstorm, get out of the water at once.

81305.q: Roughly how often a year does lightning strike the transmitter tower on the Säntis?
81305.e: The tall tower on the Säntis strongly attracts lightning. Scientists measure the strikes there.
81305.m: Lightning can strike the same place very often.

81306.q: Why are you fairly safe in a car during a thunderstorm?
a: The metal body carries the current round the outside
The rubber tyres protect you from the current
81306.e: The current flows over the car's metal body into the ground. Inside you are protected as long as you do not touch anything metal.
81306.m: In a closed car you are protected from lightning.

81307.q: Why should you not stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm?
81307.e: A lone tall tree is often the highest point for miles around. Lightning likes to strike there.
81307.m: Never stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm.

a: Lightning heats the air in an instant
Two clouds bump into each other
81308.e: Lightning makes the air very hot in an instant. The air expands with a bang, and we hear that as thunder.
81308.m: Thunder is caused by the hot air of the lightning.

81309.q: You count 9 seconds between the lightning and the thunder. Roughly how far away is the storm?
81309.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. 9 seconds divided by 3 gives 3 kilometres.
81309.m: Count the seconds and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres.

81310.q: Why does thunder often rumble for a long time instead of just banging once?
a: The sound comes from many points along the long flash
Several clouds thunder one after another
The rain makes the bang louder
The wind carries the bang round in a circle
81310.e: A flash of lightning is often several kilometres long. The sound from the parts further away arrives later, so it rumbles for a long time.
81310.m: Long rumbling comes from the long path of the lightning.

81311.q: Which Germanic god of thunder is Thursday named after?
81311.e: Donar was the god of thunder for the Germanic peoples; in the north he was called Thor. Thursday is named after him.
81311.m: Thursday is named after the thunder god Thor.

81312.q: What is the name of the Norse god who makes thunder with his hammer?
81312.e: In the old legends from Scandinavia, Thor hurls his hammer. Then there is thunder in the sky.
81312.m: Thor is the thunder god of the Norse legends.

81313.q: What does it mean if the lightning and the crash of thunder come at the same time?
81313.e: If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the lightning is only a few hundred metres away.
81313.m: If it crashes straight after the lightning, the storm is very close.

81314.q: How long should you stay under shelter after the last thunder?
81314.e: Lightning can still strike even at the end of a thunderstorm. That is why you wait about half an hour after the last thunder.
81314.m: After the last thunder, wait another half hour.

81315.q: Can you hear thunder in Switzerland in winter too?
81315.e: Thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. But occasionally there is a thunderstorm in winter too, sometimes even while it is snowing.
81315.m: It can sometimes thunder in winter too.

81316.q: What is the scale called that divides wind into forces from 0 to 12?
81316.e: The Englishman Francis Beaufort invented this scale for sailors about 200 years ago.
81316.m: Wind strength is measured on the Beaufort scale.

81317.q: What is the very strongest wind, force 12, called?
81317.e: Force 12 is the highest level. A wind like this is called a hurricane and causes great damage.
81317.m: The strongest storm is called a hurricane.

81318.q: What was the storm called that caused huge damage to forests in Switzerland on 26 December 1999?
81318.e: Lothar swept across Switzerland on St Stephen's Day 1999. It blew down millions of trees.
81318.m: Storm Lothar devastated many Swiss forests in 1999.

81319.q: What does a fast-flashing orange light on the shore of a Swiss lake mean?
81319.e: On many Swiss lakes, orange flashing lights warn of strong wind. The faster they flash, the more dangerous it is.
81319.m: Orange flashing at the lake warns of a storm.

81320.q: How does the orange light at the lake flash when a storm is coming?
81320.e: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast, about 90 times a minute. For a strong wind warning it flashes more slowly.
81320.m: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast.

a: A short, strong blast of wind
81321.e: In a gust, the wind suddenly becomes much stronger for a few seconds. Then it dies down again.
81321.m: A gust is a sudden blast of wind.

81322.q: How fast does the wind blow in a hurricane-force wind at least?
81322.e: From about 118 kilometres per hour, it is called force 12. That is as fast as a car on the motorway.
81322.m: A hurricane-force wind is as fast as a car on the motorway.

81323.q: Why should you not go into the forest during a storm?
a: Branches and trees can fall down
81323.e: Strong wind can tear off branches and blow down whole trees. That is why the forest is dangerous in a storm.
81323.m: Stay out of the forest in a storm.

81324.q: What should you do on a lake when there is a storm warning?
a: Go back to the shore at once
Go far out onto the lake
81324.e: A storm makes high waves and can tip boats over. That is why you head back to the shore at once when there is a warning.
81324.m: When there is a storm warning, go back to the shore at once.

81325.q: Are there two snowflakes that look exactly the same?
a: Yes, they all look the same
81325.e: Every snowflake grows a little differently on its way through the cloud. That is why none is exactly like another.

a: The many ice crystals reflect the light
81326.e: The many tiny crystal faces reflect all the colours of light. Together, that looks white to us.
81326.m: Snow is white because it reflects all the light.

81327.q: Why is it so quiet outside after fresh snow has fallen?
81327.e: There is a lot of air between the snowflakes. That is why fresh snow soaks up sounds like a sponge.
81327.m: Fresh snow makes the world quiet.

81328.e: Snowflakes grow high up in cold clouds. When they are heavy enough, they fall down.

81329.q: What does an ice crystal start to grow around in a cloud?
a: A grain of sand from the beach
81329.e: Tiny specks of dust float in the air. Water vapour freezes onto them and a crystal starts to grow.
81329.m: A snow crystal grows around a speck of dust.

81330.q: In what weather do especially big snowflakes fall?
a: When it is just around zero degrees
81330.e: At just around zero degrees, the crystals are a little wet. They stick together into big flakes.
81330.m: Big flakes fall when it is just around zero degrees.

a: Little pellets of snow and ice
81331.e: Graupel is small, round grains. They fall from shower clouds, usually when it is cool.
81331.m: Graupel is little grains of snow and ice.

81332.e: Graupel pellets are as small as pinheads or small peas.
81332.m: Graupel pellets are only a few millimetres big.

81333.q: How is graupel different from hail?
81333.e: Hailstones are hard and can get big. Graupel is small and soft and can easily be squashed.
81333.m: Graupel is smaller and softer than hail.

81334.q: What do graupel pellets do when they land on a hard road?
81334.e: Graupel pellets are round and light. On hard ground they bounce like little balls.

81335.q: What kind of weather do graupel showers often belong to in Switzerland?
81335.e: In April, sun, rain and cold change quickly. Then there are often short showers with graupel.
81335.m: Graupel often comes with changeable April weather.

81336.e: Graupel is white and not see-through because there is a lot of air in the pellets.

81337.q: What does graupel form from in the cloud?
81337.e: In the cold cloud, tiny water droplets freeze onto snowflakes. This is how the white pellets form.
81337.m: Graupel forms from snow and frozen droplets.

81338.q: Does graupel usually damage cars and roofs?
a: Yes, it makes everything wet and rusty
81338.e: Graupel is light and soft. It falls more slowly than hail and so rarely causes damage.

a: A smooth layer of ice on roads and paths
81339.e: With black ice, a thin, smooth layer of ice covers the ground. It is very easy to slip on it.
81339.m: Black ice is a smooth layer of ice on the ground.

81340.q: When does black ice often form?
a: When rain falls on frozen ground
81340.e: If rain falls on ground that is colder than zero degrees, it freezes into ice at once.
81340.m: Rain on frozen ground turns into black ice.

81341.q: Why can you often hardly see black ice?
a: It is as clear as glass
It is only there at night
81341.e: Black ice is completely clear and thin. You see the dark ground underneath and hardly notice the ice.
81341.m: Black ice is so clear that you can hardly see it.

81342.q: What does the winter road service spread on the roads against black ice?
81342.e: Salt makes the ice melt, even when it is a little below zero degrees.
81342.m: Road salt helps against black ice.

81343.q: What is spread on pavements so that people do not slip?
81343.e: Grit does not melt the ice. But the small stones make the ground rough so that shoes can grip.
81343.m: Grit makes slippery paths less slippery.

81344.q: Where does the road often freeze first in winter?
81344.e: Bridges are cooled by cold air from above and below. That is why they are often slippery sooner than the rest of the road.
81344.m: Bridges are often the first to be slippery.

81345.q: What helps on your shoes when it is slippery?
81345.e: Spikes and shoe chains have small metal points. They dig into the ice.

81346.q: What is the best way to walk on black ice?
a: With small steps like a penguin
81346.e: With small, flat steps your weight stays over your feet. That way you slip less.
81346.m: On black ice, walk like a penguin.

81347.q: At what temperature should you expect black ice?
81347.e: Water freezes at zero degrees. If the ground is that cold or colder, black ice can form.
81347.m: Around zero degrees, the roads get dangerous.

81348.q: What shape is a big falling raindrop?
a: Like a bread roll, flat underneath
Like a teardrop with a point
81348.e: As it falls, the air pushes against the drop from below. That is why it becomes flat underneath and looks like a bread roll.
81348.m: Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops.

81349.q: What happens to raindrops that get too big?
81349.e: From about 6 millimetres, a drop can no longer hold together. It then bursts into several smaller drops.
81349.m: Raindrops that are too big burst.

81350.q: Roughly how fast does a normal raindrop fall?
a: As fast as a racing car
81350.e: A normal raindrop falls at about 20 kilometres per hour. That is about as fast as a bike.
81350.m: A raindrop falls about as fast as a bike goes.

81351.q: What do you use to measure how much it has rained?
81351.e: A rain gauge is a container that catches the rainwater. It shows how much rain has fallen.
81351.m: A rain gauge catches the rain.

81352.q: What shape are very small raindrops?
81352.e: Small drops up to about one millimetre are held together into balls by their surface.

81353.q: What happens when lots of tiny droplets in a cloud run together?
81353.e: Cloud droplets are tiny. Only when very many run together is a raindrop heavy enough to fall.
81353.m: A raindrop is made from very many cloud droplets.

81354.q: Where does most of the water evaporate that later becomes rain?
81354.e: The oceans cover most of the Earth. That is where the sun makes the most water evaporate.
81354.m: Most rainwater comes from the oceans.

81355.q: Where does a weathercock usually sit?
a: On top of a church spire
81355.e: The weathercock sits high up so that the wind can reach it easily and everyone can see it.
81355.m: The weathercock often sits on the church tower.

a: Where the wind is blowing from
81356.e: The weathercock turns with the wind. That way you can see the wind direction.
81356.m: The weathercock shows the wind direction.

81357.q: Which way does a weathercock's beak point?
a: Towards where the wind is coming from
Towards where the wind is blowing to
81357.e: The wide tail is pushed away by the wind. That is why the head turns right into the wind.
81357.m: The weathercock faces into the wind.

81358.q: What is a weathercock usually made of?
81358.e: Weathercocks are usually made of sheet metal or copper. That way they can stand up to wind, rain and snow for many years.
81358.m: A weathercock is usually made of metal.

81359.q: Which story from the Bible does the cockerel on the church tower remind us of?
a: Peter, who denied Jesus before the cock crowed
81359.e: Jesus said Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed. According to the story, that is what happened.
81359.m: The cockerel on the church tower reminds us of Peter.

81360.q: Roughly how long have there been weathercocks on church towers?
81360.e: As early as around the year 820, a bishop in Brescia in Italy had a copper cockerel put on a church tower.
81360.m: Weathercocks have existed for over a thousand years.

81361.q: What is often fixed underneath a weathercock?
a: The letters of the compass points
81361.e: Under the cockerel there are often the letters N, E, S and W. That way you can read the wind direction exactly.
81361.m: The compass points help you read the weathercock.

81362.q: What is the general name for a turning figure on a roof that shows the wind?
81362.e: A weather vane turns with the wind. The weathercock is a particularly well-known weather vane.
81362.m: The weathercock is a weather vane.

81363.q: Where do you often see a windsock?
81363.e: Airfields are required to have a windsock. It shows the wind for take-offs and landings.

81364.q: What colours is a windsock usually?
81364.e: Windsocks usually have red and white or orange and white stripes.
81364.m: A windsock usually has red and white stripes.

81365.q: What does it mean if a windsock is stretched out completely straight?
a: There is no wind at all
81365.e: The stronger the wind blows, the more it fills the windsock. Fully stretched out means strong wind.
81365.m: A stretched-out windsock shows strong wind.

81366.q: Why is there sometimes a windsock on a motorway bridge?
a: It shows the way to the exit
81366.e: On high bridges, strong wind from the side can put cars and lorries in danger. The windsock warns drivers.
81366.m: On bridges, the windsock warns of crosswinds.

81367.q: Which way does the tip of a windsock point?
a: The way the wind is blowing to
The way the wind is coming from
81367.e: The wind blows into the big opening. So the tip points in the direction the wind is blowing.
81367.m: The tip of the windsock points with the wind.

81369.q: Why does a windsock have such eye-catching colours?
a: So pilots can see it from high up
So birds do not sit on it
81369.e: Pilots need to spot the windsock from the air. The stripes stand out well against grass and sky.
81369.m: A windsock must be visible from high up.

81370.q: What is a windsock made of?
81370.e: A windsock is a tube made of cloth. That is the only way the wind can fill it and turn it.
81370.m: A windsock is a cloth tube.

81371.q: Why do pilots need to know the wind direction?
a: Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind
Aeroplanes only fly with a tailwind
The wind shows the way to the destination
The wind forecasts the weather at the destination
81371.e: A headwind gives the aeroplane more lift on take-off and slows it down on landing. That is why the runway is used facing into the wind.
81371.m: Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind.

81372.q: Which frog used to be kept as a “weather frog”?
81372.e: In the past, people put tree frogs in jars and hoped they would give away the weather.
81372.m: The weather frog was a tree frog.

81373.q: What did people put in the weather frog's jar?
81373.e: There was a little ladder in the jar. People looked to see whether the frog was sitting at the top or the bottom.
81373.m: The weather frog had a little ladder in its jar.

81374.q: What did people think when the weather frog climbed up the ladder?
81374.e: If the frog sat at the top, people expected dry, fine weather. If it sat at the bottom, they expected rain.
81374.m: A frog at the top of the ladder was supposed to mean fine weather.

81375.q: Why does a tree frog climb upwards in fine weather?
a: Because the insects fly higher then
Because it can forecast the weather
Because it is too warm at the bottom
Because it wants to catch the sun
81375.e: In sunshine, insects fly higher, and the frog climbs after them. So it shows the weather right now, but does not forecast it.
81375.m: The tree frog climbs after its food.

81376.q: In German, who is jokingly called a “Wetterfrosch” (weather frog) today?
a: Children who play in the rain
81376.e: People who explain the weather on TV or radio are sometimes jokingly called weather frogs.
81376.m: Weather experts are jokingly called weather frogs.

81377.q: What is the federal office called that forecasts the weather in Switzerland?
81377.e: MeteoSwiss is the federal weather service. It measures the weather in many places and warns of severe weather.

81378.q: What are the well-known weather prophets from the Muota valley called?
81378.e: The Wetterschmöcker of the Muota valley forecast the weather using old signs from nature. They make their forecasts twice a year.
81378.m: The Wetterschmöcker of the Muota valley forecast the weather using signs from nature.

81379.q: Are you allowed to simply catch a tree frog in Switzerland and put it in a jar?
81379.e: In Switzerland all frogs are protected. The tree frog has also become rare.
81379.m: Tree frogs are protected and stay in the wild.

81380.q: What colour is a tree frog usually?
81380.e: The tree frog is usually light green. With the sticky pads on its toes it climbs well on leaves.
81380.m: The tree frog is bright green.

81381.e: Wood is the hard material in the trunk and branches of trees. Trees are felled and sawn into planks.
81381.m: Wood grows in the trees of the forest.

81382.q: What can you tell from the rings in a tree trunk?
81382.e: A tree forms a new annual ring every year. If you count the rings, you know how old the tree is.
81382.m: Each annual ring stands for one year of the tree's life.

81383.q: What does a dry piece of wood do in water?
81383.e: Dry wood is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why it floats on top.

81384.q: What is the craftsperson who makes furniture from wood called?
81384.e: The joiner saws, planes and glues wood into tables, cupboards and doors.
81384.m: A joiner makes furniture from wood.

81385.q: Which conifer in Switzerland loses its needles in autumn?
81385.e: In autumn the larch turns its needles golden yellow and drops them. Larch wood is very hard and lasts a long time outdoors.
81385.m: The larch has no needles in winter.

81386.q: What do Swiss wrestlers (Schwinger) fight on?
81386.e: Sawdust is produced when wood is sawn. It is soft and protects the wrestlers when they fall.
81386.m: In Swiss wrestling, soft sawdust covers the ring.

81387.q: Which tree grows most often in Swiss forests?
81387.e: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is often used for building.
81387.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.

81388.q: Why doesn't a wooden spoon in a hot pan get as hot as a metal spoon?
81388.e: Wood passes on heat only very slowly. That is why you can easily hold a wooden spoon.

81389.q: What happens to wood that stays wet for a long time?
81389.e: Fungi and tiny living things break down wet wood. It becomes soft and crumbly.

81390.q: What is glass mainly made from?
81390.e: Glass is made mainly from quartz sand. It is heated very strongly with other substances and melted.
81390.m: Glass is made from melted sand.

81391.q: About how hot does it have to be to melt glass?
81391.e: To melt sand into glass, you need a furnace at well over 1000 degrees. That is much hotter than an oven.
81391.m: Glass is only made in very great heat.

81392.q: What often happens when a drinking glass falls on a hard floor?
81392.e: Glass is hard but brittle. A hard knock breaks it into pieces.
81392.m: Glass is hard, but it breaks easily.

81393.q: What is a craftsperson called who shapes hot glass into vases using a pipe?
81393.e: The glassblower picks up liquid glass on a long pipe. Then they blow into it, and the glass becomes a ball or a vase.
81393.m: A glassblower shapes vases with their breath.

81394.q: Which part of a house is usually made of glass?
81394.e: Window panes are made of glass so that light comes into the house. Wind and rain stay outside.
81394.m: Light comes into the house through glass window panes.

81395.q: Why should you not pick up broken glass with your bare hands?
81395.e: The edges of broken glass are as sharp as a knife. It is better to sweep it up with a dustpan and brush.

81396.q: What happens to glass when it is heated very strongly?
81396.e: In great heat, glass becomes soft and thick like honey. Then it can be shaped.
81396.m: Hot glass becomes soft and can be shaped.

81397.q: What is behind the glass of a mirror?
81397.e: On the back of the mirror glass is a very thin layer of silver or aluminium. It reflects the light.
81397.m: A mirror has a shiny layer of metal at the back.

81398.q: What are colourful marbles for playing often made of?
81398.e: Many marbles are little balls of coloured glass.
81398.m: Many marbles are made of coloured glass.

81399.q: Why are railway tracks made of steel?
a: Steel is very strong and hard
81399.e: Steel is a very strong metal. The rails have to carry heavy trains without breaking.

81400.q: What does a piece of metal usually feel like when you touch it?
81400.e: Metal quickly carries the warmth of your hand away. That is why it feels cool.
81400.m: Metal feels cool because it carries heat away quickly.

81401.q: Why is there a metal wire inside an electric cable?
81401.e: Electricity flows well through metals such as copper. That is why the wires in cables are made of metal.

81402.q: What happens to metal in very great heat?
81402.e: If metal is heated strongly enough, it becomes liquid. Then it can be poured into moulds.
81402.m: In great heat, metal becomes liquid.

81403.q: What does freshly polished metal look like?
81403.e: Metals reflect a lot of light. That is why they shine when they are clean and polished.
81403.m: Polished metal shines in the light.

81404.q: Which device can you use to find metal hidden in the ground?
81404.e: A metal detector beeps when there is metal underneath it. This is how you find coins or nails in the ground.
81404.m: A metal detector beeps at metal in the ground.

a: A long thin thread of metal
81405.e: A wire is metal that has been drawn out long and thin. You can bend it.
81405.m: A wire is a thin thread of metal.

81406.q: What are most metals obtained from?
81406.e: Ore is a rock that contains metal. It is melted in a furnace to get the metal out.
81406.m: Metals are obtained from ore in rock.

81407.q: What are forks and knives usually made of?
81407.e: Cutlery is usually made of stainless steel. This is a metal that is strong and does not rust.
81407.m: Cutlery is usually made of stainless steel.

81409.q: What is plastic usually made from?
81409.e: Most plastics are made in factories from crude oil.
81409.m: Most plastics are made from crude oil.

81410.q: What is a good property of plastic?
a: It is light and easy to shape
It is as heavy as iron
81410.e: Plastic is light and can be shaped into almost any form. That is why boxes, toys and much more are made from it.
81410.m: Plastic is light and easy to shape.

81411.q: Why is plastic a problem in nature?
81411.e: Plastic does not rot like leaves. It stays in nature for many hundreds of years.
81411.m: Plastic stays in nature for a very long time.

81412.q: Does plastic grow in nature or is it made by people?
81412.e: Plastic is a synthetic, man-made material. People make it in factories.
81412.m: Plastic is a man-made material from the factory.

81413.q: Which object is usually made of plastic?
81413.e: The handle and bristles of a toothbrush are usually made of plastic. It is light and does not get soggy.
81413.m: Most toothbrushes are made of plastic.

81414.q: What happens to many plastics when they get very hot?
81414.e: Many plastics go soft in the heat and melt. That is why you don't put plastic on a hot hob.
81414.m: Many plastics go soft in the heat.

81415.q: What are fleece jumpers usually made of?
81415.e: Fleece is made of fine plastic fibres. The fabric is light, soft and warm.
81415.m: Fleece is a warm fabric made of plastic fibres.

81416.q: Why is there a plastic coating around an electric cable?
81416.e: Plastic does not let electricity through. The coating protects us when we touch the cable.
81416.m: A plastic coating protects us from electricity.

81417.q: What is paper usually made from?
81417.e: To make paper, wood is broken down into fine fibres. These are mixed with water and pressed into thin sheets.
81417.m: Paper is usually made from wood fibres.

81418.q: What did the ancient Egyptians write on before there was paper?
81418.e: Papyrus was made from the stems of a plant by the Nile. Our word paper comes from it.
81418.m: The ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus.

81419.q: What do you call thick, stiff paper for boxes?
81419.e: Cardboard is much thicker and stiffer than writing paper. Boxes and packaging are made from it.
81419.m: Boxes are often made of stiff cardboard.

81420.q: What can be made again from waste paper?
81420.e: The fibres in waste paper can be used again. That way less wood is needed for new paper.
81420.m: New paper is made from waste paper.

81421.q: Why must paper not be near a burning candle?
81421.e: Paper is thin and dry. It burns very quickly even from a small flame.

81422.q: Where does natural rubber come from?
a: From the sap of a tree
81422.e: Natural rubber is made from the milky sap of the rubber tree. The bark is cut and the sap is collected.
81422.m: Natural rubber comes from the sap of the rubber tree.

a: It is as hard as stone
81423.e: You can pull and squeeze rubber. Afterwards it goes back to its old shape.

81424.q: What do you use a rubber for?
81424.e: A rubber rubs pencil marks off the paper. That is where its name comes from.
81424.m: You remove pencil marks with a rubber.

81425.q: Why do people like wearing wellies in the rain?
a: Rubber does not let water through
81425.e: Rubber is waterproof. In wellies your feet stay dry even in puddles.

81426.q: What is the milky sap of the rubber tree called?
81426.e: The white sap of the rubber tree is called latex. Natural rubber is made from it.
81426.m: The sap of the rubber tree is called latex.

81427.q: Where does the rubber tree originally grow?
81427.e: The rubber tree comes from the rainforest by the Amazon. Today it is grown mainly in Asia.
81427.m: The rubber tree comes from the Amazon rainforest.

81428.q: What is a balloon usually made of?
81428.e: Balloons are usually made of thin rubber. That is why you can blow them up big.
81428.m: A balloon is made of thin rubber.

81429.q: Which part of a trainer is usually made of rubber?
81429.e: A rubber sole does not slip easily. It is springy and lasts a long time.
81429.m: Rubber soles don't slip so easily.

81430.q: Which animal does most wool come from?
81430.e: Sheep have a thick, curly coat. Wool is made from it.

81431.q: What do you do with wool to turn it into a thread?
81431.e: When spinning, the wool fibres are twisted into a long thread. In the past this was done with a spinning wheel.
81431.m: Wool is spun into a thread.

81432.q: What do you use to knit a woolly jumper?
81432.e: With two knitting needles, the wool is looped into stitches. Row by row, a piece of fabric grows.
81432.m: Knitting needles turn wool into stitches.

81433.q: Why does a woolly jumper keep you so nice and warm?
a: It traps a lot of air
81433.e: A lot of air gets caught between the curly wool fibres. This air holds in the body's warmth.
81433.m: The air in wool keeps us warm.

81434.q: Which animal from South America also gives very fine wool?
81434.e: Alpacas come from the Andes. Their wool is soft and warm, and there are alpacas on Swiss farms too.
81434.m: The alpaca gives soft, fine wool.

81435.q: What can happen to a woolly jumper if you wash it too hot?
81435.e: In hot water with lots of rubbing, the wool fibres mat together. The jumper shrinks and gets smaller.
81435.m: Wash wool cool, otherwise it shrinks.

81436.q: What is a thick fabric made of tightly pressed wool called?
81436.e: To make felt, wet wool is pressed and rubbed until the fibres hold firmly together. Slippers, for example, are made from it.
81436.m: Felt is made from pressed wool.

81437.q: Which part of the cotton plant provides the fibres?
