81437.e: The seeds of the plant are surrounded by white, fluffy hairs. These hairs are picked and spun into yarn.
81437.m: Cotton fibres grow on the seeds of the plant.

81438.q: Why is cotton not grown in fields in Switzerland?
a: It is too cold for it
81438.e: Cotton needs a lot of warmth and a long warm season each year. Switzerland is too cool for it.
81438.m: Cotton only grows in warm countries.

81439.q: Which trousers are usually made of cotton?
81439.e: Jeans are made of a strong cotton fabric. It is usually dyed blue.
81439.m: Jeans are made of strong cotton fabric.

81440.q: Why do people like wearing cotton T-shirts in summer?
81440.e: Cotton is soft and soaks up moisture well. That is why it feels pleasant on the skin.

81441.q: What are the little sticks with soft cotton tips at both ends called?
81441.e: Cotton wool is made from cotton. Cotton buds are used, for example, for crafts or personal care.
81441.m: Cotton buds have tips of soft cotton wool.

81442.q: Which city in eastern Switzerland became world-famous for embroidery on cotton fabric?
81442.e: Over 100 years ago, much of the world's embroidery came from the St Gallen area. It was often stitched onto fine cotton fabrics.
81442.m: St Gallen is famous for its embroidery.

81443.q: What colour are cotton fibres usually?
81443.e: Cotton on the plant looks like white cotton wool balls. Coloured fabrics are only dyed later.

81444.e: Clay is a fine, damp earth. It is easy to knead and shape.

81445.q: What do you do with shaped clay to make it really hard?
a: You fire it in a kiln
81445.e: In a very hot kiln, the clay becomes as hard as stone. Only then is it ceramics.
81445.m: Clay is fired hard in a kiln.

81446.q: What is the craftsperson who makes crockery from clay called?
81446.e: The potter shapes cups, plates and jugs from clay and then fires them.
81446.m: The potter makes crockery from clay.

81447.q: On which spinning disc are round pots shaped?
81447.e: The potter's wheel spins fast. With their hands, the potter pulls the clay up into a round pot.
81447.m: Round pots are shaped on the potter's wheel.

81448.q: What is the fine white ceramic for beautiful cups called?
81448.e: Porcelain is an especially fine and hard ceramic. It is white and sometimes almost translucent.

81449.q: What are bathroom tiles usually made of?
81449.e: Tiles are fired ceramic slabs. They are hard and easy to clean with water.
81449.m: Bathroom tiles are usually made of ceramic.

81450.q: What is the shiny layer on ceramic crockery called?
81450.e: The glaze is a thin, glass-like layer. It makes the crockery smooth, shiny and watertight.
81450.m: A glaze makes ceramics smooth and shiny.

81451.q: What are red roof tiles usually made of?
81451.e: Roof tiles are shaped from clay and fired in a kiln. They keep out rain and snow for many years.
81451.m: Red roof tiles are made of fired clay.

81452.e: Leather is animal skin that has been specially treated. This makes it last and stops it rotting.
81452.m: Leather is made from animal skin.

81453.q: What do you call turning animal skin into leather?
81453.e: In tanning, the skin is treated with special substances. Afterwards it is soft, strong and long-lasting.

81454.q: What is the craftsperson who makes and mends shoes called?
81454.e: The shoemaker, also called a cobbler, often works with leather. They sew shoes and replace old soles.

81455.q: Which object is often made of leather?
81455.e: Leather is strong and flexible at the same time. That is why belts, bags and shoes are often made from it.
81455.m: Many belts are made of leather.

81456.q: Which animal does most of the world's leather come from?
81456.e: Most leather is made from the skin of cattle. The skin is thick and large.

81457.q: What do you use to look after leather shoes so that they shine?
81457.e: Shoe polish makes the leather soft and protects it from wet. After polishing, the shoes shine.
81457.m: Shoe polish cares for leather and makes it shine.

81458.q: What was the outer cover of a football made of in the past?
81458.e: In the past, footballs were sewn from pieces of leather. Today they are mostly made of plastic.
81458.m: Old footballs were sewn from leather.

81459.q: What lies on a horse's back when riding and is often made of leather?
81459.e: The saddle is usually made of strong leather. The rider sits on it safely and comfortably.
81459.m: A saddle is usually made of leather.

81460.e: For concrete, cement, sand, gravel and water are mixed. After a while the mixture becomes rock hard.
81460.m: Concrete is made of cement, gravel and water.

81461.q: What happens to fresh concrete after a while?
81461.e: The cement combines with the water. This makes the concrete as hard as stone.
81461.m: Fresh concrete becomes rock hard over time.

81462.q: Which vehicle with a turning drum brings concrete to the building site?
81462.e: The drum of the cement mixer turns while it drives. This keeps the concrete liquid until it arrives.
81462.m: The cement mixer turns its drum while driving.

81463.q: What is put into concrete to make it even stronger?
81463.e: Steel bars in concrete make it very strong. This is called reinforced concrete.
81463.m: Steel bars make concrete even stronger.

81464.q: Which ancient people already knew a kind of concrete?
81464.e: The Romans built with a kind of concrete about 2000 years ago. One example is the huge dome of the Pantheon in Rome.
81464.m: Even the Romans built with a kind of concrete.

81465.e: Cement is a fine grey powder. Mixed with water it goes hard and holds sand and gravel together.
81465.m: Cement is a grey powder that goes hard with water.

81466.q: Which vehicle brings liquid concrete to the building site?
81466.e: The cement mixer has a big drum at the back. It turns so that the concrete doesn't go hard on the way.
81466.m: The cement mixer brings the concrete to the building site.

81467.e: Bees sweat out tiny flakes of wax from their bodies. They build their home from them.

81468.q: What do bees build from wax?
81468.e: Honeycombs are made of many six-sided cells of wax. Honey and pollen are stored in them.
81468.m: Bees build their honeycombs from wax.

81469.q: What is most candle wax made from today?
81469.e: Most candles are made of paraffin wax. This wax is made from crude oil.
81469.m: Most candles are made of paraffin wax.

81470.q: What happens to liquid wax when it cools down?
81470.e: Wax goes liquid in the warmth. When it cools down, it goes solid again.
81470.m: Liquid wax goes solid as it cools.

81471.q: What are some wheels of cheese coated with on the outside?
81471.e: A layer of wax protects the cheese from drying out and from mould. You don't eat it.
81471.m: Wax protects some cheeses from drying out.

81472.q: What do you rub on the underside of skis so that they glide better?
81472.e: Ski wax makes the underside of the skis smooth. Then they glide better over the snow.
81472.m: With ski wax, skis glide better.

81473.q: What is the thread in the middle of a candle called?
81473.e: The wick draws liquid wax upwards. There it burns with a flame.
81473.m: A candle's wick draws wax upwards.

81474.q: What do you call dipping a wick again and again into liquid wax?
81474.e: In candle dipping, the candle gets a little thicker with each dip. In Switzerland, people like to do this during Advent.
81474.m: In candle dipping, the candle gets thicker layer by layer.

81475.q: What does a layer of wax do to water on a surface?
a: It makes it run off in beads
81475.e: Wax does not like water. The drops run off in beads and don't soak in.
81475.m: Water drops run off wax in beads.

81476.q: Why do people build a bridge?
81476.e: A bridge carries a path over a river, a valley or a road. So you do not have to go through it or around it.
81476.m: A bridge leads over rivers and valleys.

81477.q: What is a bridge that hangs from thick cables called?
81477.e: On a suspension bridge, the path hangs from strong cables. The cables are firmly anchored at both ends.
81477.m: A suspension bridge hangs from strong cables.

81478.q: What is the bridge at a castle that can be pulled up called?
81478.e: The drawbridge led across the castle moat. When there was danger, it was pulled up with chains and nobody could get in.
81478.m: A drawbridge protected the castle from enemies.

81479.q: Roughly how long is the Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge in Valais?
81479.e: The pedestrian suspension bridge near Randa is 494 metres long. When it opened in 2017, it was the longest pedestrian suspension bridge in the world.
81479.m: The Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge is almost half a kilometre long.

81480.q: What shape do old stone bridges often have underneath?
81480.e: An arch carries the weight of the bridge sideways into the ground. That is why stone arches last a very long time.
81480.m: Stone bridges carry their weight with an arch.

81481.q: Which famous red bridge is in San Francisco?
81481.e: The Golden Gate Bridge is a huge suspension bridge in America. It opened in 1937 and is painted orange-red.
81481.m: The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco is red.

81482.q: According to legend, who had to be the first to cross the Devil’s Bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge?
81482.e: As payment, the Devil wanted the first soul to cross the bridge. But the clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across.
81482.m: The people of Uri tricked the Devil with a billy goat.

81483.q: What material were simple bridges over streams often made of in the past?
81483.e: There was wood everywhere in the forest. People laid tree trunks or planks across the stream.
81483.m: Simple bridges over streams used to be made of wood.

81484.q: Where do the cars drive on a motorway bridge?
81484.e: The deck is the part of the bridge you drive on. Below it, supports carry the weight.
81484.m: Cars drive on the deck of a bridge.

81485.e: A tunnel is a passage through a mountain or under the ground. Cars or trains travel through it.
81485.m: A tunnel goes right through the mountain.

81486.q: Roughly how long does it take to drive through the Gotthard Road Tunnel?
a: About a quarter of an hour
81486.e: The Gotthard Road Tunnel is almost 17 kilometres long. By car it takes about a quarter of an hour.
81486.m: Driving through the Gotthard Road Tunnel takes about a quarter of an hour.

81487.q: Which saint is regarded as the protector of tunnel builders?
81487.e: Saint Barbara is the patron saint of miners and tunnel builders. A statue of her often stands at the entrance to a tunnel construction site.

81488.q: Which huge machine bores through rock with a rotating head?
81488.e: The tunnel boring machine has a big cutting head at the front. It rotates and breaks up the rock bit by bit.
81488.m: A tunnel boring machine eats its way through rock.

81489.q: What must you have switched on when driving through a tunnel?
81489.e: In a tunnel it is darker than outside. With lights you see better and are seen better yourself.
81489.m: In a tunnel you always drive with your lights on.

81490.q: Why do people build tunnels through mountains?
a: It is nice and dark there
It is warmer to live there
81490.e: Without a tunnel you would have to drive over a high pass. The tunnel saves time and is open in winter too.
81490.m: A tunnel makes the way shorter.

81491.q: Which animal digs passages under the ground like little tunnels?
81491.e: The mole digs long passages with its broad front paws. It pushes the earth up into molehills.
81491.m: The mole digs tunnels under the meadow.

81492.q: What was used to blast the rock away when building the first Gotthard rail tunnel?
81492.e: During construction from 1872 to 1882, holes were drilled into the rock. Then they were filled with dynamite and blasted.
81492.m: For the Gotthard rail tunnel, the rock was blasted with dynamite.

a: A long bridge over a valley
81493.e: A viaduct is a long bridge, often with many arches. It carries a railway or road over a valley.
81493.m: A viaduct crosses a valley with many arches.

81494.q: Over which famous viaduct near Filisur does the train run straight into a tunnel?
81494.e: The Rhaetian Railway’s Landwasser Viaduct ends at a rock face. There the train runs straight into a tunnel.
81494.m: At the Landwasser Viaduct, the train runs straight into the mountain.

81495.q: Roughly how high is the Landwasser Viaduct?
81495.e: The Landwasser Viaduct is 65 metres high. That is about as tall as a building with 20 floors.
81495.m: The Landwasser Viaduct is 65 metres high.

81496.q: Why does the railway near Brusio in the Valposchiavo go round in a circle over a viaduct?
a: To gain height in a small space
So the train can turn round
81496.e: The railway goes a full circle and passes underneath itself. That way it gains height in a tight space.
81496.m: The Brusio spiral viaduct helps the train gain height.

81497.q: What are the old viaducts of the Rhaetian Railway built of?
81497.e: The viaducts of the Rhaetian Railway were built from natural stone more than 100 years ago. They are still standing today.
81497.m: The old viaducts in the Grisons are built of stone.

81498.q: Which railway lines in the Grisons, with many viaducts, have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008?
81498.e: The Albula line and the Bernina line of the Rhaetian Railway have been World Heritage since 2008. They cross daring viaducts through the mountains.
81498.m: The Albula and Bernina lines are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

81499.q: What do you call a Roman bridge that carried water into the city?
81499.e: In an aqueduct, water flowed in a channel across the bridge. That way fresh water came into the cities from far away.
81499.m: An aqueduct brought water into Roman cities.

81500.q: What are the tall supports under a viaduct called?
81500.e: The piers stand in the valley and carry the arches. The whole weight rests on them.

81501.q: What is the tallest building in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
81501.e: Roche Tower Building 2 in Basel is 205 metres tall. It opened in 2022 and has 50 floors.
81501.m: Switzerland’s tallest building is in Basel.

81502.q: In which city is the tallest building in the world (as of 2025)?
81502.e: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is 828 metres tall. That is four times as tall as the tallest building in Switzerland.
81502.m: The tallest building in the world is in Dubai.

81503.q: What do you call a very, very tall high-rise building?
81503.e: A skyscraper is so tall that it seems to touch the clouds. The word comes from English.
81503.m: Very tall high-rise buildings are called skyscrapers.

81504.q: What happens to a very tall high-rise building in strong wind?
81504.e: Tall buildings are built so that they give a little in the wind. That way they do not break.
81504.m: Tall buildings sway a tiny bit in the wind.

81505.q: In which American city are there many famous high-rise buildings in the district of Manhattan?
81505.e: Manhattan is a district of New York. A great many famous high-rise buildings stand close together there.
81505.m: There are many famous high-rise buildings in New York.

81506.q: Why do red lights shine at night on top of very tall buildings?
a: As a night light for birds
81506.e: The red lamps show pilots at night that there is a tall obstacle there.
81506.m: Red lights warn aircraft about tall buildings.

81507.q: Why do people build high-rise buildings in big cities?
a: Because there are no trees there
Because the ground is too soft
Because they want to ban the view
81507.e: In cities, land is scarce and expensive. Building upwards saves a lot of space.
81507.m: High-rise buildings save a lot of space in the city.

81508.q: What are the separate levels in a high-rise building called?
81508.e: A high-rise building has many floors on top of each other. You count them upwards from the ground floor.
81508.m: A high-rise building has many floors.

81509.q: What does a high-rise building absolutely need for emergencies?
a: A staircase as an escape route
A swimming pool on the roof
81509.e: In a fire you must not use the lift. Everyone can get outside safely by the stairs.
81509.m: In an emergency, you escape a high-rise building by the stairs.

81510.q: What do building workers wear on their heads for protection on the building site?
81510.e: On a building site, things can fall down. The hard helmet protects the head.
81510.m: On a building site you wear a hard hat.

81511.q: Why do building workers wear bright orange vests?
a: So they can be seen easily
So they do not get cold
81511.e: The bright colour stands out at once. That way drivers of machines and cars see the workers in time.
81511.m: Hi-vis vests make building workers easy to see.

81512.q: Who draws the plans for a new house?
81512.e: The architect plans what the house should look like. The tradespeople then build it according to the plans.
81512.m: Architects draw the plans for houses.

81513.q: What do you dig first before building a house with a cellar?
81513.e: A cellar needs a big hole in the ground. This building pit is dug out right at the start.
81513.m: At the start you dig out a building pit.

81514.q: Who builds walls out of bricks on a building site?
81514.e: The bricklayer lays brick on brick and joins them together. That makes solid walls.
81514.m: The bricklayer builds walls out of bricks.

81515.q: Which shoes do building workers wear to protect their toes?
81515.e: Safety boots have a hard cap at the front. If something heavy falls on them, the toes stay unharmed.

81516.q: In Switzerland, what do wooden poles in a meadow show before a house is built?
a: How big the house will be
Where there is water in the ground
81516.e: These poles are called building profiles. That way everyone can see where the new house will stand and how tall it will be.
81516.m: Building profiles show the size of a new house.

81517.q: Which celebration is held in Switzerland when the roof frame of a new house is up?
81517.e: At the topping-out ceremony, the owners thank the tradespeople. Often a decorated little fir tree is then put on the roof.
81517.m: The topping-out ceremony is held when the roof frame is up.

81518.q: What do you need a crane for on a building site?
81518.e: A crane lifts heavy things such as steel girders or stones. It takes them exactly where they are needed.
81518.m: A crane lifts heavy loads up high.

81519.q: Where does the crane operator often sit on a big building crane?
a: In the cellar of the house
81519.e: The cab is at the top of the crane. From there the crane operator has a good view of the building site.
81519.m: The crane operator often sits high up in the cab.

81520.q: What is the long arm of a crane called?
81520.e: A trolley moves back and forth along the jib. The rope with the load hangs from it.
81520.m: The long arm of a crane is called the jib.

81521.q: Why does a crane have heavy concrete blocks on its short end?
a: So it does not tip over
81521.e: The concrete blocks are a counterweight to the load on the long arm. That way the crane stays balanced.
81521.m: A counterweight stops the crane from tipping over.

81522.q: What does the load hang from on a crane?
a: A hook on a steel cable
81522.e: A strong steel cable with a hook carries the load. A winch pulls the cable up or lets it down.
81522.m: The load hangs from the crane hook on a steel cable.

81523.q: What is the tall crane whose top can turn in a circle called?
81523.e: The tower crane has a tall tower. At the top, the jib turns all the way round over the whole building site.
81523.m: A tower crane turns over the whole building site.

81524.q: Which long-necked bird is the crane named after?
81524.e: The long arm of the crane is reminiscent of the long neck of the bird called a crane. That is why it has this name.
81524.m: The crane got its name from the bird.

81525.q: Why must a building crane not work in very strong wind?
a: The birds get in the way
81525.e: Strong wind makes the load swing back and forth. Then it becomes dangerous for the workers below.
81525.m: In a storm, cranes stand still.

81526.q: What is a brick made of?
81526.e: Bricks are shaped from damp loam or clay. Then they are dried and made hard.
81526.m: Bricks are made from loam or clay.

81528.e: Clay contains iron. When fired, it turns the bricks red or reddish-brown.

81529.q: What does the bricklayer use to join the bricks together?
81529.e: Mortar is a paste of sand, binder and water. It sets hard and holds the bricks together.
81529.m: Mortar holds the bricks of a wall together.

81530.q: What do you call a structure built of bricks?
81530.e: When you stack bricks on top of each other and join them, you get a wall.
81530.m: Lots of bricks make a wall.

81531.q: Why are the bricks in each row laid offset?
81531.e: If each brick lies over two bricks in the row below, the weight is spread out. That way the wall holds much better.
81531.m: Offset bricks make a wall stable.

81532.q: Why do many bricks in Switzerland have holes?
81532.e: The holes make the bricks lighter. The air inside them also keeps the warmth in the house.

81533.q: Which flat tool does a bricklayer use to spread mortar between the bricks?
81533.e: The bricklayer’s trowel is a flat blade with a handle. With it the bricklayer picks up the paste and smooths it out.
81533.m: The bricklayer works with a trowel.

81534.q: What does a dam hold back?
81534.e: A dam blocks off a valley. Behind it, the water collects to form a reservoir.
81534.m: A dam holds back water to form a lake.

81535.q: What is the lake behind a dam called?
81535.e: The water of a river collects behind the dam. That creates an artificial lake: the reservoir.
81535.m: Behind a dam there is a reservoir.

81536.q: What is the very top edge of a dam called?
81536.e: The top part of the dam is called the crest. On many dams you can walk along the crest.
81536.m: The top edge of a dam is called the crest.

81537.q: What shape are many dams in narrow mountain valleys?
81537.e: An arch dam curves towards the lake. It directs the pressure of the water into the rock walls on the left and right.
81537.m: A curved dam braces itself against the rock walls.

81538.q: What is the water behind many dams in Switzerland used for?
81538.e: The water flows down through pipes to turbines. These turn and produce electricity.
81538.m: Water from reservoirs is used to make electricity.

81539.q: What are modern dams mostly built of?
81539.e: Large dams are made of huge amounts of concrete. It is heavy, solid and withstands the water.
81539.m: Modern dams are made of concrete.

81540.q: What is the dam in the Verzasca Valley in Ticino famous for?
81540.e: Brave people jump more than 200 metres down from the Verzasca Dam on an elastic rope.
81540.m: People bungee jump from the Verzasca Dam.

81541.q: Why is a dam much thicker at the bottom than at the top?
a: The water presses harder at the bottom
It is warmer at the bottom
There is no concrete at the top
The workers live at the bottom
81541.e: The deeper the water, the harder it presses. That is why the dam has to be especially thick at the bottom.
81541.m: The water presses hardest at the bottom.

81542.q: Why are there warning signs on some rivers below dams?
81542.e: When a power station releases water, the river rises quickly. That is why you should not stay in the riverbed there.
81542.m: Below dams, a river can suddenly swell.

81544.q: Apart from crossing the river, what was the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne used for in the past?
81544.e: The bridge was part of Lucerne’s city wall. From there the city could be defended from the lake side.
81544.m: The Chapel Bridge used to protect the city of Lucerne.

81545.q: Where did the pile dwellers build their houses?
a: On lake shores and in moors
81545.e: The pile dwellers lived thousands of years ago on the shores of lakes and in moors. Their houses stood on wooden piles.
81545.m: Pile dwellings stood on lake shores and in moors.

81546.q: Why did the pile dwellers’ houses stand on piles?
81546.e: The water level of the lakes rose and fell. On piles, the houses stayed dry above the wet ground.
81546.m: On piles, the houses stayed dry.

81547.q: Roughly how old are the pile dwellings in Switzerland?
81547.e: The pile-dwelling settlements around the Alps date from about 5000 to 500 BC.
81547.m: The pile dwellings are many thousands of years old.

81548.q: Where did people in the pile-dwelling period build their houses?
a: On lake shores, on wooden piles
In caves high in the mountains
81548.e: The pile dwellings stood on wooden piles on lake shores and in moors. Since 2011, 111 sites around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
81548.m: Pile dwellings stood on piles on the lake shore.

81549.q: The pile dwellings are World Heritage. What does that mean?
a: They matter to the whole world and are protected
You may build houses there again
They belong to a single family
81549.e: World Heritage Sites are especially valuable places in the world. They are protected so that people in the future can still see them.
81549.m: The pile dwellings are a protected World Heritage Site.

81550.q: What did the pile dwellers build their houses from?
81550.e: The pile dwellers felled trees for piles and walls. They sealed the walls with loam and covered the roofs with reeds or bark.
81550.m: Pile dwellers built with wood, loam and reeds.

81551.q: Why are the pile dwellers’ wooden finds still so well preserved today?
81551.e: In the wet ground by the lake, no air reached the wood. That is why it did not rot.
81551.m: In wet ground, old wood is preserved for a long time.

81552.q: What is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree trunk called?
81552.e: The pile dwellers hollowed out a thick tree trunk. They used this dugout canoe to travel across the lake.
81552.m: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single tree trunk.

81553.q: What are experts who search the ground for old traces of people called?
81553.e: Archaeologists dig carefully in the ground and examine the finds. That is how we learn how the pile dwellers lived.
81553.m: Archaeologists study old finds from the ground.

81554.q: Why does a house need foundations?
81554.e: The foundations spread the heavy weight of the house over the ground. That way the house does not sink or tilt.
81554.m: Good foundations keep the house straight.

81555.q: What are foundations mostly made of today?
81555.e: Today, foundations are poured from concrete. It is very solid and does not rot in damp ground.
81555.m: Foundations are poured from concrete today.

81556.q: Which part of a house is built first?
81556.e: Without a firm base you cannot build walls. That is why you start right at the bottom.
81556.m: You build a house from the bottom up.

81557.q: Why does a high-rise building need especially strong foundations?
81557.e: A high-rise building weighs a great deal. That is why its foundations often reach deep into the ground.

81558.q: What do many old houses in Venice stand on?
81558.e: The ground in Venice is soft and wet. So millions of wooden piles were driven into it, and houses were built on top.
81558.m: Venice stands on lots of wooden piles.

81559.q: What does the saying “built on sand” mean?
81559.e: A house on loose sand has no firm hold. That is why people say this when something could easily collapse.
81559.m: Something built on sand does not stand firm.

81560.q: Why must foundations lie deep enough in the ground?
a: So frost does not damage them
81560.e: In winter the top of the ground can freeze and lift. Further down it stays frost-free, and the house stands steady.
81560.m: Foundations lie deeper than the frost reaches.

81561.q: Why do people put scaffolding up against a house?
a: So you can work safely up high
So the house does not fall over
81561.e: On the scaffolding, tradespeople can work on the outside wall, for example painting or fitting windows.
81561.m: Scaffolding is a safe place to work up high.

81562.q: What is scaffolding in Switzerland mostly made of today?
81562.e: Modern scaffolding is made of steel or aluminium tubes. It can be put up and taken down quickly.
81562.m: Modern scaffolding is made of metal tubes.

81563.q: Which plant was traditionally used to build scaffolding in Hong Kong?
81563.e: Bamboo is light, flexible and very strong. In Hong Kong it was used even on tall buildings, but since 2025 it has gradually been replaced there by metal.
81563.m: In Hong Kong, scaffolding was made of bamboo for a long time.

81564.q: What is often hung on scaffolding so nothing falls onto the street?
81564.e: Nets and tarpaulins catch dust and small pieces. That way people on the pavement are protected.
81564.m: Nets on scaffolding protect people on the pavement.

81565.q: What stops workers on scaffolding from falling off?
81565.e: On the outside, the scaffolding has a guardrail. You can hold on and you do not fall off.
81565.m: A guardrail on scaffolding prevents falls.

81566.e: Painters paint the walls of houses from the scaffolding. That way they can safely reach high places too.
81566.m: Tradespeople work up high on scaffolding.

81567.q: What is laid on the tubes of scaffolding so you can walk on it?
81567.e: Firm boards or metal platforms are laid on the tubes. The tradespeople stand on them.
81567.m: On scaffolding you walk on firm boards.

81568.q: Why is scaffolding fixed to the wall of the house?
a: So it does not tip over
81568.e: Tall scaffolding is narrow and can tip over in the wind. That is why it is anchored firmly to the wall.
81568.m: Scaffolding is anchored to the wall of the house.

81569.q: For 8 + 5 you want to add up to exactly 10 first. How do you split the 5?
81569.e: 8 + 2 makes exactly 10. Then you work out 10 + 3 and get 13.
81569.m: When crossing ten, you first add up to the ten.

81570.q: What is 7 + 6 if you add across the ten?
81570.e: 7 + 3 makes 10. That leaves 3 of the 6, so 10 + 3 equals 13.

81571.q: Which way of working out 9 + 4 goes exactly through 10?
81571.e: 9 + 1 makes 10. The 4 is split into 1 and 3, so 10 + 3 equals 13.
81571.m: Nine is only one away from ten.

81572.q: For 14 − 6 you first work out 14 − 4 and get to 10. How much more do you have to take away?
81572.e: 6 is split into 4 and 2. After 14 − 4 equals 10, you take away 2 more and get 8.
81572.m: With subtraction, too, you go back to the ten first.

81573.q: Crossing ten when subtracting: what is 15 − 7?

81574.q: What is 38 + 5 if you add across the ten 40?
81574.m: Crossing ten works with bigger numbers too.

81575.q: What is 62 − 8 if you go back through 60?
81575.m: First subtract down to the ten, then the rest.

81576.q: Which sum makes you cross a ten?
81576.e: 8 + 7 makes 15 and goes past 10. The other answers, 9, 18 and 14, stay in the same ten.
81576.m: If the answer slips into a new ten, you are crossing a ten.

81577.q: Which sum stays in the same ten, without crossing a ten?
81577.e: 23 + 4 makes 27 and stays in the twenties. The other sums go past the next ten.
81577.m: Without crossing a ten, the tens digit stays the same.

81578.q: How much is missing from 70 to 100?
81578.m: Seventy and thirty make a hundred together.

81579.q: How much is missing from 45 to 100?
81579.e: 45 + 5 makes 50, and 50 + 50 makes 100. Altogether 5 + 50 equals 55 is missing.
81579.m: Forty-five and fifty-five make a hundred.

81580.q: Which number makes 38 up to exactly 100?
81580.e: 38 + 2 makes 40, and 40 + 60 makes 100. So 2 + 60 equals 62 is missing.
81580.m: When adding on, you go to the next ten first.

81581.q: Lena pays for a chewing gum costing 65 centimes with one franc. How many centimes does she get back?
81581.e: One franc is 100 centimes. 65 + 35 makes 100, so she gets 35 centimes back.
81581.m: A franc has a hundred centimes.

81582.q: How much is missing from 99 to 100?
81582.e: 99 is the number just before 100. Only 1 is missing.
81582.m: Ninety-nine plus one makes a hundred.

81583.q: Which pair of numbers adds up to exactly 100?
81583.e: 40 + 60 makes 100. The other pairs make 110, 90 and 110.
81583.m: Forty and sixty are partners to a hundred.

81584.q: From 27 to 30 you need 3. How much more do you need from 30 to 100?
81584.e: 30 + 70 makes 100. So from 27 to 100 you need 3 + 70 equals 73 altogether.
81584.m: You can add on to a hundred in two steps.

81585.q: Which number must you add to 81 to get 100?
81585.e: 81 + 9 makes 90, and 90 + 10 makes 100. So you need 9 + 10 equals 19.
81585.m: Eighty-one and nineteen make a hundred.

81586.q: A book has 100 pages. Tim has already read 12 pages. How many pages does he still have to read?
81586.e: 12 + 88 makes 100. So he still has 88 pages to go.
81586.m: Twelve and eighty-eight make a hundred.

81587.e: 3 hundreds and 4 hundreds are 7 hundreds, so 700.
81587.m: You calculate with hundreds just like with ones.

81588.e: 9 hundreds minus 5 hundreds is 4 hundreds, so 400.
81588.m: Nine hundred minus five hundred makes four hundred.

81589.e: 6 hundreds plus 2 hundreds are 8 hundreds. So you work out 6 + 2 and add two zeros.
81589.m: A small sum helps with the big sum in hundreds.

81590.e: 4 hundreds and 6 hundreds are 10 hundreds. 10 hundreds make 1000.
81590.m: Four hundred and six hundred make a thousand together.

81591.q: A bike costs 400 francs and a helmet 100 francs. How much do both cost together?
81591.e: 4 hundreds and 1 hundred are 5 hundreds. Together they cost 500 francs.
81591.m: You work out amounts in hundreds like small numbers and add two zeros.

81592.q: How much is missing from 700 to 1000?
81592.m: Seven hundred and three hundred make a thousand.

81593.e: 2 + 3 + 1 makes 6. So it is 6 hundreds, which means 600.
81593.m: You can add hundreds one after the other.

81594.e: 1000 is 10 hundreds. 10 hundreds minus 2 hundreds are 8 hundreds, so 800.
81594.m: A thousand minus two hundred makes eight hundred.

81595.q: Which times tables are often called the key facts?
81595.e: The facts for times 1, times 2, times 5 and times 10 are easy to remember. You can work out the other facts from them.
81595.m: You can work out difficult multiplications from the key facts.

81596.q: How does the key fact 5 · 6 = 30 help with 6 · 6?
81596.e: 6 · 6 is one more six than 5 · 6. So 30 + 6 equals 36.
81596.m: One more step in a times table means adding the number once more.

81597.q: With the key fact 10 · 7 = 70 you can find 9 · 7. What is 9 · 7?
81597.e: 9 · 7 is one seven less than 10 · 7. So 70 − 7 equals 63.
81597.m: Nine times a number is ten times the number minus the number once.

81598.e: 5 is half of 10. So 5 · 8 is half of 80, which is 40.
81598.m: Five times a number is half of ten times the number.

81599.q: Which key fact helps most with 4 · 7?
81599.m: Four times a number is double two times the number.

81600.q: What is 6 · 7 if you know that 5 · 7 = 35?
81600.e: 6 · 7 is one more seven than 5 · 7. So 35 + 7 equals 42.

81601.q: What is 4 · 9 if you know that 5 · 9 = 45?
81601.e: 4 · 9 is one nine less than 5 · 9. So 45 − 9 equals 36.

81602.q: What is 8 · 6 if you know that 10 · 6 = 60?
81602.e: 8 · 6 is two sixes less than 10 · 6. So 60 − 12 equals 48.

81603.q: What is the swapped sum of 3 + 8?
81603.e: In the swapped sum, the two numbers change places. 3 + 8 becomes 8 + 3, and the answer stays 11.
81603.m: In a swapped sum, the numbers change places.

81604.q: What is the swapped sum of 4 · 7?
81604.m: With multiplication, too, you may swap the numbers.

81605.q: For which calculation does swapping the numbers give a different answer?
81605.e: 9 − 4 makes 5, but 4 − 9 does not make 5. With plus and times, the answer stays the same when you swap.
81605.m: With subtraction you cannot simply swap the numbers.

81606.q: What is the swapped sum of 2 + 49 that is easier to work out?
81606.e: It is easier to count on from the bigger number. 49 + 2 makes 51, just like 2 + 49.
81606.m: When adding, it is handy to start with the bigger number.

81607.q: When adding, what happens to the answer if you swap the numbers?
81607.e: 5 + 3 and 3 + 5 both make 8. The order does not change the answer when adding.
81607.m: When adding, the answer stays the same if you swap the numbers.

81608.e: 9 · 3 is the swapped version of 3 · 9. So the answer is also 27.
81608.m: A swapped sum has the same answer as the original.

81609.q: An egg box has 2 rows of 6 eggs. If you turn it, you see 6 rows of 2 eggs. Which equation fits?
81609.e: There are always the same number of eggs, namely 12. So 6 · 2 equals 2 · 6.
81609.m: If you turn a dot pattern, the number stays the same.

81610.e: In 5 + 7 and 7 + 5, only the numbers are swapped. 12 − 7 would be an inverse calculation.
81610.m: Swapped sums have the same numbers in a different order.

81611.q: Which calculation is the inverse of 6 + 3 = 9?
81611.e: The inverse calculation goes back the way you came. You take the 3 away from 9 again and get 6.
81611.m: The inverse calculation undoes a calculation.

81612.q: Which calculation is the inverse of 4 · 5 = 20?
81612.e: Times and divide belong together. 20 divided by 5 makes 4 again.
81612.m: Every multiplication has a division as its inverse.

81613.q: Which calculation checks whether 15 − 6 = 9 is right?
81613.e: If you add the 6 back to the answer 9, you must get 15. That works, so the calculation is right.
81613.m: You can check an answer with the inverse calculation.

81614.q: In ? + 7 = 12 a number is missing. Which inverse calculation helps you find it?
81614.e: You work backwards: 12 − 7 makes 5. So the 5 is missing.
81614.m: You can often find a missing number with the inverse calculation.

81615.e: Going backwards, 3 · 4 = 12 becomes 12 : 4 = 3. Division is the inverse of multiplication.
81615.m: Division is the inverse of multiplication.

81616.e: Going backwards, 8 + 2 = 10 becomes 10 − 2 = 8. Subtraction is the inverse of addition.
81616.m: Subtraction is the inverse of addition.

81617.q: In ? · 6 = 42 a number is missing. Which number is it?
81617.e: The inverse calculation is 42 : 6. That makes 7, because 7 · 6 equals 42.
81617.m: With division you find the missing number in a multiplication.

81618.e: If you multiply the answer 8 by 4 again, you get 32. That is how you check the division.
81618.m: Every division has a multiplication as its inverse.

81619.q: Number chain: start at 5, first + 3 and then · 2. Where do you end up?
81619.m: In a number chain, you calculate step by step.

81620.q: Number chain: start at 20, first − 5 and then + 8. What is the result?
81620.m: In a number chain, the answer becomes the new starting number.

81621.q: Number chain: start at 4, first · 3 and then − 2. What is the target number?
81621.m: In a number chain you must keep to the order of the steps.

81622.q: Number chain: start at 30, first : 3 and then + 5. What do you get?
81622.m: Any operation can appear in a number chain.

81623.q: Number chain: start at 10 and add 10 three times in a row. Which number does it end at?
81623.m: If you add ten three times, you move on three tens.

81624.q: In a number chain, the step + 6 leads to the number 15. Which number was at the start?
81624.e: You work backwards: 15 − 6 makes 9. Check: 9 + 6 equals 15.
81624.m: You find a missing starting number by working backwards.

81625.q: Number chain: start at 50, first − 20 and then : 3. Where do you end up?
81625.m: A number chain can also get smaller.

81626.q: Number chain: start at 7, · 2, then + 6, then : 2. What does the chain give?
81626.m: You solve long number chains step by step too.

81627.q: A child holds up 9 fingers. How many fingers are folded down?
81627.e: Altogether it has 10 fingers. 10 − 9 makes 1, so one finger is folded down.
81627.m: Folded and raised fingers make ten together.

81628.q: A whole hand shows 5. How many fingers of the second hand do you need as well to show 8?
81628.e: 5 + 3 makes 8. So you raise 3 more fingers on the second hand.
81628.m: With a full hand and a few fingers you can show numbers up to ten.

81629.q: In the nines finger trick, you fold down the fourth finger for 4 · 9. There are 3 fingers on the left and 6 on the right. Which answer do the hands show?
81629.e: The fingers on the left count as tens, the fingers on the right as ones. 3 tens and 6 ones make 36.
81629.m: In the nines finger trick, the fingers on the left show the tens.

81630.q: In the nines finger trick, you fold down the seventh finger for 7 · 9. How many fingers are left standing to its left?
81630.e: There are 6 fingers to the left of the seventh finger and 3 to the right. That makes 63, and 7 · 9 is 63.
81630.m: In the nines finger trick, you fold down the finger for the number you are multiplying.

81631.q: Why is our counting in tens probably linked to our hands?
81631.e: People have 10 fingers and counted on their fingers very early on. That is probably why we group in tens.
81631.m: Our base-ten system matches our ten fingers.

81632.q: A child works out 4 + 3 on their fingers. How many fingers are up at the end?
81632.e: First the child raises 4 fingers, then 3 more. That makes 7 fingers altogether.
81632.m: You can count small additions on your fingers.

81633.q: Someone shows 10 fingers and folds down 4 of them. Which calculation fits?
81633.e: 4 of the 10 fingers are taken away. 6 fingers stay up.

81634.q: Three children hold up all their fingers. How many fingers is that?

81635.q: What happens to a number like 6 when you multiply it by 10?
a: A zero is added at the end
A zero is added at the front
81635.e: 6 · 10 makes 60. Each digit moves one place to the left, and a zero goes at the end.
81635.m: Times ten adds a zero to whole numbers.

81637.m: Thirty-four times ten makes three hundred and forty.

81638.e: 90 is 9 tens. Divided by 10, 9 is left.
81638.m: Dividing a multiple of ten by ten removes the zero at the end.

81639.e: With 500 divided by 10, one zero disappears. 50 is left.
81639.m: Five hundred divided by ten makes fifty.

81640.q: How many 10-franc notes do you need for 80 francs?
81640.e: A 10-franc note is worth 10 francs. 80 : 10 makes 8 notes.

81641.q: A pack has 10 coloured pencils. How many pencils are in 6 packs?
81641.e: 6 packs of 10 pencils are 6 · 10, so 60 pencils.
81641.m: Six packs of ten are sixty.

81642.q: One franc, which is 100 centimes, is shared fairly among 10 children. How much does each child get?
81642.e: 100 : 10 makes 10. So each child gets a 10-centime coin.
81642.m: Dividing by ten makes a number ten times smaller.

81643.m: Twenty-five times ten makes two hundred and fifty.

81644.q: For 34 + 25 you first work out 30 + 20 and then 4 + 5. What is the answer?
81644.e: 30 + 20 makes 50 and 4 + 5 makes 9. Together that is 59.
81644.m: With partly written methods, you work out tens and ones separately.

81645.q: What is 47 + 30 if you only add the tens?
81645.e: 47 + 30 means adding 3 tens. 4 tens become 7 tens, so 77.
81645.m: If only tens are added, the ones stay the same.

81646.q: What is 56 + 27 if you first add 20 and then 7?
81646.m: You can add a number in steps.

81647.q: What is 85 − 32 if you first take away 30 and then 2?
81647.m: With subtraction, too, you can take away in steps.

81648.q: What is 73 − 45 if you work it out in steps?
81648.m: Taking away the tens first and then the ones makes it easier.

81649.q: How do you work out 6 · 14 with a partly written method in two parts?
81649.e: 14 is 10 + 4. You work out 6 · 10 equals 60 and 6 · 4 equals 24. Together that is 84.
81649.m: You can split a big multiplication into two small ones.

81650.q: What is 3 · 23 if you work out 3 · 20 and 3 · 3?
81650.e: 3 · 20 makes 60 and 3 · 3 makes 9. Together that is 69.
81650.m: When multiplying, you can work out tens and ones separately.

81651.q: What is 48 : 4 if you work out 40 : 4 and 8 : 4?
81651.e: 40 : 4 makes 10 and 8 : 4 makes 2. Together that is 12.
81651.m: Splitting the number helps with division too.

81652.q: What is 125 + 240 if you add the hundreds, tens and ones separately?
81652.e: 100 + 200 makes 300, 20 + 40 makes 60 and 5 + 0 makes 5. Together that is 365.
81652.m: You can add hundreds, tens and ones separately.

81653.q: Which split of the number 10 is correct?
81653.e: 6 + 4 makes 10. The other pairs make 11, 11 and 9.
81653.m: Six and four are number bonds to ten.

81654.q: Into which two equal numbers can you split 18?
81654.e: 9 + 9 makes 18. The other pairs make 16, 12 and 20.
81654.m: Eighteen is made of two nines.

81655.e: 73 has 7 tens and 3 ones. So 73 equals 70 + 3.
81655.m: You can split a two-digit number into tens and ones.

81656.q: The number 7 is to be split into two numbers. Which split is correct?
81656.m: Five and two make seven together.

81657.q: You share 5 marbles between your left and right hand. One hand may also be empty. How many possibilities are there?
81657.e: The left hand can hold 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 marbles. The right hand has the rest. That makes 6 possibilities.
81657.m: If you search in order, you find all the ways to split a number.

81658.q: In the number house, 9 is at the top. Bottom left is 4. Which number goes next to it on the right?
81658.e: The two bottom numbers add up to the roof number. 4 + 5 makes 9.
81658.m: In the number house, the bottom numbers add up to the roof number.

81659.q: How do you split 245 into hundreds, tens and ones?
81659.e: 245 has 2 hundreds, 4 tens and 5 ones. That is 200 + 40 + 5.
81659.m: Each digit has a different value depending on its place.

81660.q: Which split of 12 is made of three equal numbers?
81660.e: 4 + 4 + 4 makes 12. The others add up to 9, 18 and 12, but 5, 5 and 2 are not equal.
81660.m: You can split twelve into three fours.

81661.q: 6 + 7 is nearly a double. Which method fits?
81661.e: 7 is one more than 6. So you work out 6 + 6 equals 12 and then add 1, making 13.
81661.m: With neighbouring numbers, doubling plus one helps.

81662.q: What is 8 + 9 using the trick “double plus one”?

81663.q: What is 25 + 26 if you double 25 first?
81663.m: Doubling plus one works with bigger neighbouring numbers too.

81664.q: Which sum can you solve with “double plus one”?
81664.e: 5 and 6 are neighbouring numbers. 5 + 5 makes 10, plus 1 makes 11.
81664.m: Double plus one works when two numbers are right next to each other.

81665.q: For 7 + 8 you can also work out 8 + 8. What must you do afterwards?
81665.e: 8 + 8 makes 16. Because 7 is one less than 8, you take away 1 and get 15.
81665.m: You can also double the bigger number and then take away one.

81667.q: What is 15 + 16 using the trick “double plus one”?

81668.m: Fifty plus fifty-one makes a hundred and one.

81669.q: What is a secret code for?
a: So only people in the know can read it
81669.e: A secret code makes a message unreadable for strangers. Only someone who knows the secret can read it.
81669.m: A secret code protects a message from strangers' eyes.

81670.q: What do you need to make a secret code readable again?
81670.e: The key reveals how the message was changed. With it you can change it back.
81670.m: Without the key, a secret code remains a puzzle.

81671.q: Which juice can you use to write an invisible secret message?
81671.e: Lemon juice is almost colourless. On white paper you can hardly see the writing once it has dried.
81671.m: Lemon juice works as invisible ink.

81672.q: How do you make a message written in lemon juice visible again?
a: You put the paper in water
You put the paper in the fridge
You fold the paper up very small
81672.e: Heat turns the dried juice brown and the writing appears. Only do this with an adult's help.
81672.m: Heat makes lemon writing brown and readable.

a: To read a message out loud
To copy a message out neatly
81673.e: When encrypting, the message is changed so that strangers cannot understand it.
81673.m: Encrypting turns a message into ciphertext.

a: To hide a message in the garden
81674.e: When decrypting, the ciphertext is changed back with the key. Then you can read the message again.
81674.m: Decrypting is the way back from ciphertext to the message.

81675.q: What is the science of encrypting messages called?
81675.e: The word comes from Greek and means roughly “secret writing”.

81676.q: What do you call someone who works out a secret code without the key?
81676.e: A code breaker looks for patterns in the ciphertext and works out how it was encrypted.
81676.m: Code breakers solve secret codes without the key.

81677.q: Why should you not tell everyone the key to a secret code?
81677.e: Anyone who knows the key can read the secret message. That is why it stays secret.
81677.m: You keep the key to a secret code secret.

81678.q: Which famous Roman is the Caesar cipher named after?
81678.e: The historian Suetonius reports that Julius Caesar encrypted his letters in this way.
81678.m: The Caesar cipher bears the name of Julius Caesar.

81679.q: By how many letters is Caesar said to have shifted the alphabet?
81679.e: According to Suetonius, instead of each letter Caesar wrote the letter three places further on in the alphabet.
81679.m: Caesar shifted each letter by three places.

81680.q: What does the receiver of a Caesar message need to know to decrypt it?
a: By how many places it was shifted
81680.e: The number of places is the key. With it, the receiver shifts each letter back again.
81680.m: In the Caesar cipher, the number of places is the key.

81681.q: Each letter is shifted 1 place further along. What does the word “DOG” become?
81681.e: D becomes E, O becomes P and G becomes H. This gives EPH.
81681.m: With a shift of one, you always take the next letter.

81682.q: An animal's name was shifted by 3 places and now reads “ZROI”. Which animal is it?
81682.e: You go back 3 places for each letter: Z becomes W, R becomes O, O becomes L and I becomes F. This gives WOLF.
81682.m: To decrypt, you shift the letters back.

81683.q: With a shift of 3 places, after Z you come back to the beginning. What does Z become?
81683.e: After Z, the alphabet starts again at A. Three steps on from Z are A, B, C.
81683.m: In the Caesar cipher, the alphabet goes round in a circle.

81684.q: How many different shifts make sense with an alphabet of 26 letters?
81684.e: You can shift by 1 to 25 places. A shift of 26 places gives the same text again.
81684.m: Having few possibilities makes the Caesar cipher easy to crack.

81685.q: Which tool with two rotating rings of letters helps with Caesar encryption?
81685.e: With a cipher wheel, you turn the inner ring against the outer one. That way you can read off the shifted letter for each letter.
81685.m: A cipher wheel shows shifted letters at a glance.

81686.q: The word “MUM” is shifted 2 places further along. What comes out?
81686.e: M becomes O, U becomes W and M becomes O. This gives OWO.
81686.m: With a shift of two, you always skip one letter.

81687.q: What are the signs of the freemasons' cipher made of?
81687.e: Each letter belongs to a space in a grid. You only draw the lines around the space, sometimes with a dot.
81687.m: The freemasons' cipher is made of pieces of grids and dots.

81688.q: Which two basic shapes do you draw for the freemasons' cipher?
a: A grid like in noughts and crosses and an X
81688.e: The letters are shared out among the spaces of a cross-shaped grid and a diagonal cross.
81688.m: In the freemasons' cipher, the letters sit in grids and crosses.

81689.q: By which English name, meaning a pen for pigs, is the freemasons' cipher also known?
81689.e: The spaces in the grid are like the pens in a stable. That is why the code is called “Pigpen” in English.
81689.m: The freemasons' cipher is called Pigpen in English.

81690.q: What do the dots in the freemasons' cipher tell apart?
a: Letters with the same grid shape
81690.e: Two letters can have the same grid shape. Only the dot shows which one is meant.
81690.m: A dot turns a grid shape into a different letter.

81691.q: Who often used this grid code in the 18th century and gave it its name?
81691.e: The Freemasons are a society with their own customs. In the 18th century they often used this code.
81691.m: The freemasons' cipher is named after the Freemasons.

81692.q: Where do you often come across the freemasons' cipher today?
81692.e: Because the signs look mysterious, the code is often used in puzzle games today.
81692.m: The freemasons' cipher is a popular puzzle code today.

81693.q: Is the freemasons' cipher a secure form of encryption?
a: No, it is easy to crack
Yes, only computers can read it
No, because it has no signs at all
81693.e: Each letter always has the same sign. Anyone who knows the grids or looks for patterns can read the text quickly.
81693.m: The freemasons' cipher is a fun code and not secure encryption.

81694.q: How many spaces does a noughts and crosses grid, as used for the freemasons' cipher, have?
81694.e: Two vertical and two horizontal lines form 3 times 3 spaces. That is 9 spaces.
81694.m: A noughts and crosses grid has nine spaces.

81695.q: What can you use to read mirror writing easily?
81695.e: If you hold mirror writing up to a mirror, it appears the right way round in the mirror.
81695.m: Mirror writing is best read in a mirror.

81696.q: Which famous artist and inventor wrote many notes in mirror writing?
81696.e: Leonardo da Vinci was left-handed. Much of his notebooks is written in mirror writing.
81696.m: Leonardo da Vinci wrote in mirror writing.

81697.q: Why is there a word in mirror writing on the front of some ambulances?
a: So it can be read in the rear-view mirror
Because it is cheaper that way
81697.e: Anyone driving in front of the ambulance sees it in the rear-view mirror. There the word appears the right way round.
81697.m: Mirror writing on ambulances is made for the rear-view mirror.

81698.q: What does the word “OTTO” look like in mirror writing?
81698.e: OTTO reads the same backwards, and the letters O and T are the same on both sides. That is why the mirror changes nothing.
81698.m: Some words look exactly the same in a mirror.

81699.q: In which direction does mirror writing run?
81699.e: Our normal writing runs from left to right. Mirror writing runs exactly the other way.
81699.m: Mirror writing runs from right to left.

81700.q: Which capital letter looks exactly the same when mirrored?
81700.e: The A is the same on the left and right. R, F and S face the other way in a mirror.
81700.m: Letters with matching halves look the same in a mirror.

81701.q: Which small letter becomes a “d” when mirrored?
81701.e: With b the round part is on the right, with d on the left. In a mirror, left and right swap.
81701.m: Mirrored, a b becomes a d.

81702.q: What advantage does mirror writing have for some left-handed people?
a: Their hand does not smudge the fresh ink
You do not need a pen
81702.e: If you write with your left hand from right to left, your hand moves away from what you have written. That way nothing smudges.
81702.m: Mirror writing can save left-handers from smudging.

81703.q: Who invented the writing system for blind people made of dots you can feel?
81703.e: Louis Braille was blind himself. The dot writing is named after him.
81703.m: Braille is named after Louis Braille.

81704.q: How many dots make up a character in normal braille?
81704.e: Each character has room for 6 dots. Depending on which dots are raised, a different letter is formed.

81705.q: How do blind people read braille?
81705.e: The dots are raised. You run your fingertips over them and feel the characters.
81705.m: You read braille with your fingers.

81706.q: Which country did Louis Braille come from?
81706.e: Louis Braille was born in 1809 in Coupvray near Paris.

81707.q: Roughly how old was Louis Braille when he had finished his dot writing?
81707.e: Braille was born in 1809 and finished his writing system in 1825. He was then about 16 years old.
81707.m: Louis Braille invented his writing system as a teenager.

81708.q: How did Louis Braille lose his sight as a small child?
a: Through an accident in his father's workshop
Through a fall from a horse
81708.e: At the age of three he injured his eye with a sharp tool. Later he went completely blind.
81708.m: Louis Braille went blind because of an accident.

81709.q: Where do you often find Braille?
81709.e: Many medicine packets have the name written in Braille. That way blind people can find the right medicine too.
81709.m: Braille helps blind people in everyday life.

81710.q: Where do you find Braille in many lifts?
a: On the floor of the lift
On the ceiling of the lift
81710.e: Next to or on the buttons in a lift there are often Braille dots. That way blind people can find the right floor.
81710.m: Braille in a lift shows blind people the floors.

81711.q: The dots of Braille are pressed into the paper. What do they feel like?
81711.e: The dots are pressed into the paper from behind. On the front they stick out as small bumps.
81711.m: Braille dots stick out of the paper.

81712.q: What do you use to give signals in flag semaphore?
81712.e: In flag semaphore a person holds flags in their hands and moves their arms.
81712.m: In flag semaphore you talk with flags.

81713.q: Where was flag semaphore mainly used?
81713.e: With flag semaphore, ships could communicate with each other or with people on land.
81713.m: Flag semaphore is a signalling language of seafaring.

81714.q: In flag semaphore, what shows which letter is meant?
81714.e: Each letter has its own position of the two arms. So you read the position of the arms.
81714.m: In flag semaphore, the arm position shows the letter.

81715.q: What colours are semaphore flags on ships?
81715.e: The flags used at sea are divided diagonally into a yellow and a red triangle. That way you can see them from far away.
81715.m: Semaphore flags on ships are yellow and red.

81716.q: What do ships mostly use today to communicate instead of semaphore flags?
81716.e: With radio you can talk over long distances, even when you cannot see each other. Semaphore flags are now only rarely needed.
81716.m: Radio has largely replaced signalling with flags.

81717.q: How many flags does a person hold in flag semaphore?
81717.e: The person holds one flag in each hand. That makes two altogether.
81717.m: In flag semaphore you hold one flag in each hand.

81718.q: Which sense do you use to receive a message in flag semaphore?
81718.e: You have to see the flag signals. That is why you need a clear view between the people.
81718.m: Flag semaphore is a message for the eyes.

81719.q: What is another name for flag signalling with the arms?
81719.e: Semaphore means roughly “sign bearer”. That is the name for signals given with arms or flags.
81719.m: Flag signalling is also called semaphore.

81720.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on: which number goes with E?
81720.e: E is the fifth letter of the alphabet: A, B, C, D, E. So 5 goes with it.
81720.m: In the letter-number code you count the letters of the alphabet.

81721.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2 and so on: which number goes with Z?
81721.e: The alphabet has 26 letters. Z is the last one, so it gets the number 26.
81721.m: The last letter, Z, has the number twenty-six.

81722.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2 and so on: which letter has the number 13?
81722.e: Count along: A is 1, ... L is 12, M is 13.
81722.m: The letter M is in the middle of the alphabet.

81724.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2 and so on: how do you write “BAD”?
81724.e: B is 2, A is 1 and D is 4. So you write 2 1 4.
81724.m: To encode, you replace each letter with its number.

81726.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2 and so on: what is the sum of the numbers of “ABC”?
81726.e: A is 1, B is 2 and C is 3. 1 + 2 + 3 makes 6.
81726.m: You can also add up the numbers of a code word.

81727.q: In the code A = 1, B = 2 and so on: which number goes with J?
81727.e: J is the tenth letter of the alphabet. That is why 10 goes with it.
81727.m: The letter J has the number ten.

81729.q: Binary cards have 1, 2, 4 and 8 dots. How many dots does the next card have?
81729.e: Each card has twice as many dots as the one before. Double 8 is 16.
81729.m: With binary cards the number of dots doubles from card to card.

81730.q: With binary cards, how do you get the number of dots on a card from the card before?
81730.e: The card with 2 dots has twice as many as the card with 1 dot, the card with 4 twice as many as the one with 2. And so it goes on.
81730.m: Each binary card has twice as many dots as its neighbour.

81731.q: There are binary cards with 8, 4, 2 and 1 dots. Which cards together show exactly 5 dots?
81731.e: 4 + 1 makes 5. The other pairs make 9, 6 and 3.
81731.m: With binary cards you add up the dots on the face-up cards.

81732.q: With the binary cards 8, 4, 2 and 1, the cards 8 and 2 are face up. Which number is shown?
81732.e: You only count the face-up cards: 8 + 2 makes 10.
81732.m: Binary cards that are turned over do not count.

81733.q: What is the biggest number you can show with the binary cards 1, 2, 4 and 8?
81733.e: If all the cards are face up, you add 8 + 4 + 2 + 1. That makes 15.
81733.m: With all cards face up you reach the biggest number.

81734.q: With the cards 4, 2 and 1, a face-up card means 1 and a turned-over card means 0. How do you write the number 6?
81734.e: 6 is 4 + 2. The cards 4 and 2 are face up, the 1 is turned over. That gives 110.
81734.m: With face-up and turned-over cards you write numbers with zeros and ones.

81735.q: With the cards 8, 4, 2 and 1, 1001 stands for “up, down, down, up”. Which number is that?
81735.e: The cards 8 and 1 are face up. 8 + 1 makes 9.

81736.q: With the binary cards 4, 2 and 1, how many face-up cards do you need for the number 7?
81736.e: 7 is 4 + 2 + 1. So you need all three cards face up.
81736.m: For seven, the cards four, two and one are face up.

81737.q: Which symbol on many power buttons was made from a 1 and a 0?
81737.e: The symbol shows a line in an open circle. The line stands for 1, meaning “on”, the circle for 0, meaning “off”.
81737.m: The on/off symbol combines the one and the zero.

81738.q: What is the smallest unit of information in a computer, which can be 0 or 1, called?
81738.e: The bit is the smallest unit a computer calculates with. The word comes from “binary digit”.
81738.m: A bit is the smallest unit in a computer.

81739.q: How many bits make one byte?
81739.e: A byte is made of 8 bits. With it you can store a letter, for example.

81740.q: A light switch can be off or on. Which digit usually stands for “on” in binary code?
81740.e: In binary code, 1 usually means “on” and 0 means “off”.
81740.m: One stands for switched on, zero for switched off.

81741.q: How many different values can a single bit have?
81741.e: A bit is either 0 or 1. There are no other possibilities.
81741.m: A bit has exactly two possibilities.

81742.q: What is the number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1 called?
81742.e: Binary means “made of two parts”. The binary system manages with the two digits 0 and 1.
81742.m: In the binary system there are only zeros and ones.

81743.q: What does a computer store as zeros and ones?
81743.e: Everything in a computer is translated into bits, including photos, songs and letters.
81743.m: For a computer, even pictures and music are just zeros and ones.

81744.q: What is a QR code made of?
81744.e: A QR code is made of small dark and light squares. Like zeros and ones, together they store information.
81744.m: A QR code stores information with light and dark squares.

81745.e: A pictogram shows information with a simple picture. You do not need to be able to read for it.
81745.m: A pictogram explains something with a picture.

81746.q: Why do people from many countries understand pictograms?
81746.e: A picture can be understood in any language. That is why pictograms are useful at railway stations and airports.
81746.m: People understand pictograms without a shared language.

81747.q: What colour is the sign with the running figure for the emergency exit?
81747.e: Emergency exits are marked with a green sign and a running figure.
81747.m: The emergency exit is marked with a green sign.

81748.q: What does a pictogram with a crossed-out cigarette mean?
81748.e: A red line through a picture means something is not allowed. So smoking is not allowed here.
81748.m: A crossed-out picture means something is not allowed.

81749.q: For which sporting event are new pictograms designed for all the sports every time?
81749.e: At the Olympic Games there are many sports and visitors from all over the world. Pictograms show them the way to each sport.
81749.m: The Olympic Games get their own sports pictograms every time.

81750.q: What does a pictogram with a knife and fork on the motorway mean?
81750.e: You need a knife and fork for eating. The sign points to a restaurant.
81750.m: A knife and fork stand for a restaurant.

81751.q: Which picture sign on a mobile phone usually stands for “call”?
81751.e: The receiver reminds us of old telephones. That is why it stands for calls.

81752.q: What does a pictogram with a wheelchair show?
a: A place for people in wheelchairs
81752.e: The wheelchair sign shows, for example, a toilet or a parking space made for people in wheelchairs.
81752.m: The wheelchair pictogram shows places for people in wheelchairs.

81753.q: What is a check digit for?
81753.e: The check digit is calculated from the other digits. If it does not match, there is a mistake somewhere.
81753.m: A check digit reveals mistakes in a number.

81754.q: Where is the check digit in a barcode on a product in a shop?
81754.e: In a shop barcode, the last digit is the check digit. It is calculated from the digits before it.
81754.m: In a barcode, the last digit is the check digit.

81755.q: What usually happens at the till if the check digit of a barcode does not match?
a: The scanner does not accept the code
81755.e: The scanner recalculates the check digit. If it does not match, something was read wrongly and the code is not accepted.
81755.m: With the check digit the till notices when something was read wrongly.

81756.q: In a simple code, the last digit is the sum of the others. Which digit goes after 2 3 4?
81756.e: 2 + 3 + 4 makes 9. So 9 is the check digit.
81756.m: A check digit is calculated from the other digits.

81757.q: In a simple code, the last digit is the sum of the others. Which code contains a mistake?
81757.e: 1 + 2 makes 3, not 4. In the others the sum is correct.
81757.m: If the check digit is wrong, there is a mistake in the code.

81758.q: Which typing mistake is often caught by a good check digit?
a: A screen that is too small
81758.e: Good check digits are calculated so that the result changes when two digits swap places.
81758.m: Check digits also catch swapped digits.

81759.q: Which number for a Swiss bank account has two check digits right after “CH”?
81759.e: A Swiss IBAN starts with CH followed by two check digits. That way typing mistakes in payments are caught.
81759.m: The IBAN has check digits against typing mistakes.

81760.q: On which object do you find an ISBN with a check digit?
81760.e: The ISBN is a book's number. Its last digit is a check digit.
81760.m: Every book has an ISBN with a check digit.

81761.q: Which letter does the code word “Alfa” stand for in the international spelling alphabet?
81761.e: In the international spelling alphabet each word stands for its first letter. Alfa stands for A.
81761.m: Alfa stands for the letter A.

81762.q: Which code word stands for B in the international spelling alphabet?
81762.e: The words are Alfa, Bravo, Charlie and so on. Bravo stands for B.
81762.m: Bravo stands for the letter B.

81763.q: Which letter does the code word “Zulu” stand for in the international spelling alphabet?
81763.e: Zulu is the last word of the spelling alphabet and stands for Z.
81763.m: Zulu stands for the letter Z.

81764.q: Why do people use a spelling alphabet on the radio or phone?
a: So that letters are not mixed up
81764.e: Letters like B and P sound similar. With whole words you understand them for sure.
81764.m: A spelling alphabet prevents misunderstandings when spelling.

81765.q: What is a code word that you agree on with your family?
a: A secret password to recognise each other
81765.e: A code word is a word that only people in the know have. You use it to recognise each other.
81765.m: A code word is a secret word to recognise each other.

81766.q: What can a family code word be useful for?
a: Checking whether someone really comes from your parents
81766.e: If a stranger says your parents sent them, you ask for the code word. If they do not know it, you do not go with them.
81766.m: A family code word helps you recognise safe people.

81767.q: Who may you tell your family code word to?
a: Only the people who should know it
All the children in the playground
81767.e: A code word only works as long as it stays secret. That is why only a few trusted people know it.
81767.m: A code word is only useful if it stays secret.

81768.q: Which code word stands for S in the international spelling alphabet?
81768.e: In the international spelling alphabet Sierra stands for S. Other examples are Tango for T and Delta for D.
81768.m: Sierra stands for the letter S.

81769.q: What colour are the flowers of the snowdrop?
81769.e: The snowdrop has white flowers. They look like little bells.

81770.q: In which months does the snowdrop usually flower?
81770.e: The snowdrop is one of the first spring flowers. It usually flowers in February and March.
81770.m: The snowdrop already flowers in February.

81771.q: What does the snowdrop grow from again every year?
81771.e: The snowdrop has a small bulb in the ground. Food for the next year is stored in it.
81771.m: The snowdrop grows from a bulb.

81772.q: What colour are the small marks on the inner petals of the snowdrop?
81772.e: The three shorter inner petals each have a green mark. The outer petals have no mark.
81772.m: The snowdrop has green marks inside.

81773.q: Which way does the snowdrop flower point?
81773.e: The flower hangs down, nodding. That way the pollen stays dry in rain and snow.

81774.q: Why is the snowdrop called that?
a: It often flowers while there is still snow
It is only green in winter
81774.e: The snowdrop flowers very early in the year, often between patches of leftover snow. Its flower hangs down like a drop.
81774.m: The snowdrop sometimes flowers in the snow.

81775.e: All parts of the snowdrop are poisonous, especially the bulb. You can look at them, but not eat them.

81776.q: How many petals does a snowdrop have?
81776.e: The snowdrop has three long outer petals and three short inner ones. Together that makes six.

81777.q: Which animals already find food on snowdrops in February?
81777.e: On warm days the first bees fly out. They collect pollen from snowdrops.
81777.m: Snowdrops are early food for bees.

81778.q: What does a crocus grow from?
81778.e: The crocus has a small, round corm in the ground. It stores food in it for the next spring.
81778.m: The crocus grows from a corm.

81779.e: Crocuses are often purple. They also come in white and yellow.

81780.q: Which expensive spice comes from a kind of crocus?
81780.e: Saffron comes from the saffron crocus. It is one of the most expensive spices in the world.
81780.m: Saffron comes from the saffron crocus.

81781.q: In which village in Valais is saffron grown?
81781.e: The village of Mund in Upper Valais is known for its saffron. Saffron crocuses grow there in small fields.
81781.m: Saffron grows in Mund in Valais.

81782.q: What do crocus flowers do in the evening or when it rains?
81782.e: Crocuses open in sunshine and warmth. In the evening and in bad weather they close their flowers again.
81782.m: The crocus closes its flower in the rain.

81783.q: Where do lots of wild crocuses flower in Switzerland in spring?
81783.e: Wild crocuses flower in meadows in the mountains, often just after the snow melts. Some meadows then turn completely white and purple.
81783.m: Wild crocuses flower in mountain meadows.

81784.q: Which part of the saffron crocus is used as a spice?
a: The red threads in the flower
81784.e: The spice is the red threads from the middle of the flower. They are picked by hand and dried.
81784.m: Saffron is the red threads of the crocus flower.

81785.q: What do crocus leaves look like?
81785.e: Crocuses have narrow, grass-like leaves. They often have a pale stripe down the middle.
81785.m: The crocus has narrow leaves like grass.

81786.q: When do most garden crocuses flower?
81786.e: Garden crocuses flower in early spring, from about February to April. They are among the first colourful flowers of the year.

81787.q: In which month does the spring snowflake often start to flower?
81787.e: The spring snowflake flowers from February and above all in March. That is why its German name means “March cup”.
81787.m: The spring snowflake flowers in March.

81788.q: What is the main colour of the spring snowflake’s flowers?
81788.e: The flowers of the spring snowflake are white. They hang down like little cups.
81788.m: The spring snowflake has white flowers.

81789.q: Where are the green or yellow spots on the spring snowflake?
a: At the tips of the petals
81789.e: Each petal has a small green or yellow spot at its tip. It looks like a dab of paint.
81789.m: The spring snowflake has spots at the tips of its petals.

81790.q: How can you easily recognise the spring snowflake?
a: All its petals are the same length
It has no leaves at all
81790.e: All six petals of the spring snowflake are the same length. That is what makes it different from the snowdrop.
81790.m: The spring snowflake’s petals are all the same length.

81791.q: Where does the spring snowflake like to grow?
81791.e: The spring snowflake likes damp soil. You find it in floodplain forests and by streams.
81791.m: The spring snowflake loves damp woods.

81792.q: How many flowers does a spring snowflake stem usually have?
81792.e: A stem usually has one flower, sometimes two. They hang down.
81792.m: The spring snowflake usually has one flower per stem.

81793.q: What should you do with wild spring snowflakes in the woods?
81793.e: The spring snowflake has become rare and is protected in many places. So you leave it standing and enjoy it.
81793.m: Leave wild spring snowflakes where they are.

81794.q: Which other white spring flower is the spring snowflake often mixed up with?
81794.e: The spring snowflake and the snowdrop both flower early in the year and have white, hanging flowers. But the spring snowflake is bigger.
81794.m: The spring snowflake looks like the snowdrop.

81795.q: What colour are the flowers of the wood anemone usually?
81795.e: The wood anemone usually has white flowers. On the outside they are sometimes a little pink.
81795.m: The wood anemone has white flowers.

81796.q: In which months does the wood anemone usually flower?
81796.e: The wood anemone flowers in spring, usually in March and April. The trees are still bare then, and lots of light reaches the ground.
81796.m: The wood anemone flowers in March and April.

81797.q: What does the wood anemone have under the ground?
a: A big tuber like a potato
81797.e: A horizontal rootstock grows under the ground. New plants sprout from it every spring.
81797.m: The wood anemone has a rootstock.

81798.q: How do wood anemones often grow in the woods?
a: As a big carpet of flowers
81798.e: Wood anemones often grow close together. This makes a big carpet of flowers.
81798.m: Wood anemones often form a carpet of flowers.

81799.e: The wood anemone is poisonous. Its sap can even irritate the skin.

81800.q: How many petals does the wood anemone usually have?
81800.e: The flower usually has six petals, sometimes up to eight. Yellow stamens sit in the middle.
81800.m: The wood anemone usually has six petals.

81801.q: About how tall does a wood anemone grow?
81801.e: The wood anemone is a small plant. It only grows about 10 to 25 centimetres tall.
81801.m: The wood anemone is a small plant.

81802.q: Why is the wood anemone also called “windflower”?
a: Its delicate flowers move in even a little wind
81802.e: The flowers sit on thin stalks. Even a light wind makes them sway to and fro. The Latin name Anemone also comes from the Greek word for wind.
81802.m: Wood anemone flowers sway in the wind.

81803.q: What colour are the flowers of the cowslip?
81803.e: The cowslip has yellow flowers. Inside they often have small orange spots.

81804.q: In German the cowslip is called the “key flower”. Why?
a: The flowers look like a bunch of keys
It grows next to front doors
It is as hard as metal
It only grows on house walls
81804.e: Several flowers hang together at the top of the stem. This is like a bunch of keys.
81804.m: The cowslip looks like a bunch of keys.

81805.q: What is another old name for the cowslip?
81805.e: The cowslip is also called keys of heaven. The name comes from an old legend.
81805.m: The cowslip is also called keys of heaven.

81806.q: In which months does the cowslip usually flower?
81806.e: The cowslip flowers in spring, above all in April and May.
81806.m: The cowslip flowers in April and May.

81807.q: Where do you often find the cowslip?
81807.e: The cowslip likes to grow in sunny meadows and at the edge of woods.

81808.q: Which group of plants does the cowslip belong to?
81808.e: The cowslip is a primrose. The colourful primroses that you buy in pots in spring are related to it.

81809.q: How many flowers sit at the top of a cowslip stem?
81809.e: Several flowers sit together at the top of the stem. They all lean to the same side.
81809.m: The cowslip has several flowers on one stem.

81810.q: According to an old legend, who dropped the keys of heaven?
81810.e: According to the legend, St Peter dropped the keys to heaven. Where they fell to Earth, cowslips grew.
81810.m: In a legend, St Peter lost the keys of heaven.

81811.q: What colour are the flowers of the hepatica usually?
81811.e: The hepatica usually has blue to blue-violet flowers. It glows in the still bare woods.

81812.q: Why is the hepatica also called liverleaf?
a: Its leaves remind people of a liver
81812.e: The leaves are lobed and often reddish underneath. In the past their shape reminded people of a liver.
81812.m: The leaves of the hepatica look like a liver.

81813.q: How many lobes does a hepatica leaf have?
81813.e: The hepatica leaf is divided into three rounded lobes. This lets you recognise the plant even without a flower.
81813.m: The hepatica leaf has three lobes.

81814.q: In which months does the hepatica usually flower?
81814.e: The hepatica is an early spring flower. It flowers above all in March and April.
81814.m: The hepatica flowers in March and April.

81815.q: Can you eat a fresh hepatica?
81815.e: The fresh hepatica is poisonous. You should not put it in your mouth.

81816.q: What can you see in the middle of the hepatica flower?
81816.e: Lots of small whitish stamens sit in the middle. They shine brightly out of the coloured flower.

81817.q: What do the old leaves of the hepatica do in winter?
81817.e: The leaves of the hepatica stay green through the winter. After flowering, new leaves grow.
81817.m: The hepatica stays green in winter.

81818.q: Which flower colour is also found in the hepatica, but rarely?
81818.e: The hepatica usually has coloured flowers. Rarely you can also find completely white flowers.
81818.m: The hepatica rarely has white flowers.

81819.q: What does wild garlic smell of?
81819.e: Wild garlic smells strongly of garlic. In spring you can often smell it in the woods from far away.

81820.q: Which part of wild garlic do people usually eat?
81820.e: With wild garlic people mainly eat the fresh green leaves. They taste spicy.
81820.m: With wild garlic you eat the leaves.

81821.q: What is often made from wild garlic in the kitchen?
